documents.t: The best-kept secret about Claude Code is that it respects ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN. Set them to your gateway and Claude Code stops talking to api.anthropic.com directly — it talks to your proxy, which forwards to Anthropic (or anywhere else) with the auth you control. For a team, this changes three things at once: One shared virtual key per developer. You issue and revoke keys in the proxy UI. No shared root credentials in .env files. Per-developer budgets and logs. The proxy tags every request, so "who spent the $300 yesterday" is a database query, not an incident. Model aliasing. You can pin claude-sonnet-4-6 at the proxy so a model deprecation is a one-line config change, not a repo-wide grep. Start a minimal proxy in three steps: Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Install LiteLLM with the proxy extra⌄ In a fresh venv or via uv: uv tool install 'litellm[proxy]'. This pulls in the gateway server (FastAPI + admin UI) alongside the client SDK. ←PreviousNext→ 2Author a config.yaml that lists the Claude models you want to expose⌄ Model IDs on the left are the ALIAS your callers see (whatever you want); the litellm_params.model on the right is the REAL provider route. Put your ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the env, not the file. ←PreviousNext→ 3Start the proxy and point Claude Code at it⌄ Run litellm --config config.yaml (default port 4000). Then set ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to the proxy URL and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN to a virtual key. Claude Code will route every call through the proxy without knowing. ←PreviousNext→ The config file that makes this work: config.yaml — Claude Sonnet/Opus/Haiku behind LiteLLM CopyOpen in Claude↗ model_list: - model_name: claude-opus-4-7 litellm_params: model: anthropic/claude-opus-4-7 api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY - model_name: claude-sonnet-4-6 litellm_params: model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6 api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY - model_name: claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 litellm_params: model: anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY litellm_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY # Optional: enable exact-match prompt caching cache: true cache_params: type: redis host: os.environ/REDIS_HOST Then, from any developer's shell: Point Claude Code at the proxy (per-developer .env) CopyOpen in Claude↗ export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="https://llm.internal.example.com" export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="sk-team-alice-9f4c..." # a VIRTUAL key issued by the proxy # now every Claude Code call goes through YOUR gateway claude --model claude-sonnet-4-6 The non-obvious win is the virtual key. The master key is admin-only and never ships to laptops. Each developer gets a virtual key that maps to only the models you allow, has its own monthly budget, and can be revoked in seconds without rotating the underlying Anthropic key. If a laptop is lost, you kill one row in Postgres — not the whole team's access. Careful: the same env vars work with Anthropic's Bedrock and Vertex integrations, but there are edge cases with experimental beta features. For Bedrock deployments the LiteLLM docs recommend setting CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS=1 in ~/.claude/settings.json to avoid header-compatibility issues.
documents.s: Killer workflow: point Claude Code at your own LiteLLM proxy

documents.t: If you don't want to host anything, OpenRouter's fallback array is the shortest path to "silently retry another model when Claude 429s". You send an ordered list; OpenRouter walks it top-down and returns the first model that answered. Claude → GPT → Gemini fallback in one request (OpenRouter) CopyOpen in Claude↗ import openai client = openai.OpenAI( api_key="YOUR_OPENROUTER_KEY", base_url="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1", ) response = client.chat.completions.create( model="anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.5", extra_body={ # Ordered fallback. If the first model 429s, is down, or is # rejected by moderation, OpenRouter tries the next one. "models": [ "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.5", "openai/gpt-5.4", "google/gemini-2.5-pro", ], }, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain B-trees in one paragraph."}], ) # 'model' in the response tells you which one actually answered. print(response.model, "->", response.choices[0].message.content) Three things people miss on their first try: Billing follows the model that answered, not the one you asked for. If Claude fails and GPT-5.4 answers, you pay OpenRouter's GPT-5.4 rate for that request. The fallback triggers on more than 5xx. Rate-limiting, provider downtime, context-length validation errors, and content-moderation refusals all promote to the next model. That last one is the sharpest edge — a "moderation" refusal from one provider can silently route to a more permissive one, which may or may not be what you want. Review your fallback list with the same care as an ACL. You cannot mix models with fallbacks. The Anthropic-format Messages endpoint uses a different fallbacks array. Sending both keys in the same request returns a 400. Pick the format your client speaks and stick to it.
documents.s: Killer workflow #2: silent fallback with OpenRouter

documents.t: On 24 March 2026 at 10:39 UTC, two malicious PyPI releases of LiteLLM — v1.82.7 and v1.82.8 — were published by an attacker after they stole the maintainer's PyPI credentials via a prior compromise of Trivy, a security scanner running in LiteLLM's CI/CD pipeline. PyPI quarantined the packages at 13:38 UTC (about three hours later). During the exposure window, tens of thousands of downloads occurred. The payload was an infostealer with a persistence mechanism (a litellm_init.pth file that ran on every Python invocation, harvested credentials, and installed a systemd backdoor). Attribution goes to a group tracked as TeamPCP, which also compromised Trivy and Checkmarx KICS. If you run LiteLLM in any environment, apply this once and then keep it in your platform playbook: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Pin to a known-safe version⌄ v1.82.6 and earlier are clean. v1.83.0 and later (published via LiteLLM's rebuilt CI/CD v2 pipeline) are clean. Anything in between should be uninstalled and the environment considered tainted. The official Docker image (ghcr.io/berriai/litellm) was NOT compromised — the incident was PyPI-only. ←PreviousNext→ 2Check for the persistence file⌄ Grep site-packages for litellm_init.pth. If it exists, treat the machine as compromised: rotate every credential that was present in env vars or on disk (Anthropic, OpenAI, cloud, DB, SSH, K8s tokens) and forensic-scan for the systemd backdoor. ←PreviousNext→ 3Verify Docker image signatures with cosign⌄ From v1.83.0-nightly onward, LiteLLM signs its images. Verifying with cosign before rollout catches a repeat of this incident at the container layer. ←PreviousNext→ 4Prefer the container image over pip install in production⌄ The Docker image escaped the attack; the PyPI wheel did not. That's a durable signal: for a networked service that holds API keys, running the pinned container is safer than a pip-installed venv on a shared host. ←PreviousNext→ 5Add outbound egress alerting⌄ The malware phoned home to models.litellm[.]cloud and checkmarx[.]zone — neither is legitimate. Egress allowlists on production LLM proxies catch this class of attack early. ←PreviousNext→ The wider lesson isn't "don't use LiteLLM" — it's "assume every dependency in your AI stack, including security scanners, can be a delivery vector." Pin versions, sign images, and put your gateway on a network segment that only reaches the model providers. Last verified: 2026-07-27. Safe-version guidance verified on the date above against LiteLLM's official incident post and the PyPI incident report. Before installing or upgrading LiteLLM in production, re-check the current safe versions and any follow-up CVEs from the vendor's security page. Confirm against the official source.
documents.s: The March 2026 LiteLLM supply-chain incident: what to actually do

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1How many providers, and who runs the infra?⌄ One or two providers with a small team → skip the gateway; direct SDKs are fine. Three+ providers OR a team where 'who has the key' matters → gateway. If you have DevOps and privacy requirements, self-host LiteLLM or Portkey OSS. If you'd rather pay someone else to run it, OpenRouter (hosted-only) or Vercel AI Gateway (great if you already deploy there). ←PreviousNext→ 2Do you need virtual keys, budgets, and per-team spend?⌄ Yes → LiteLLM (native, mature) or Portkey (native, plus semantic caching). No → OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway are lighter. ←PreviousNext→ 3Do you need to route between providers in ONE request?⌄ OpenRouter's models[] and Vercel AI Gateway's provider-options fallbacks are the shortest path. LiteLLM does it too via fallbacks: in the config, but writes closer to a rules engine than a one-line array. ←PreviousNext→ 4Is Claude Code the primary consumer?⌄ Then LiteLLM wins by a mile — it's the only gateway with first-class docs for the ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL + virtual-key pattern, so a team of ten Claude Code users behind one proxy just works. ←PreviousNext→ 5Are you regulated / air-gapped?⌄ Self-hosted only: LiteLLM proxy container or Portkey OSS via npx @portkey-ai/gateway. Egress-allowlist the proxy to the providers it's authorised to reach. ←PreviousNext→ Common combinations that ship in production: Solo dev / prototype: OpenRouter direct. One key, 300+ models, done. Small team, Claude-first: LiteLLM proxy with Anthropic + one fallback provider, virtual keys per engineer, Redis prompt caching. Vercel-native product: Vercel AI Gateway with the AI SDK; add OpenRouter as a provider-options fallback for exotic models. Regulated / EU: Self-hosted LiteLLM or Portkey OSS in-VPC with Presidio PII masking in front (see Claude + Local Models for the redaction pattern). AI-product with heavy repeat traffic: Portkey (semantic caching commonly drives 30–50% cost reduction on chat-style workloads, per Portkey's own case studies — verify on your traffic before believing headline numbers).
documents.s: Choose the right gateway for your situation

documents.t: Gateways are middleware — they change how you reach models, not which model is right. Two things still need real work: Prompt portability. Claude, GPT, and Gemini answer the same prompt differently, and system-prompt conventions vary. A gateway doesn't rewrite your prompt for the fallback provider — that's what Porting prompts across models and Cross-AI translation are for. Evals. The gateway makes it easy to A/B two models on the same request. It cannot tell you which one was actually better on YOUR task. Run a real eval (see Evals) before switching defaults. A common mistake is to install a gateway and consider "multi-model" done. The gateway is the transport layer; portability and evals are the product layer. Check yourself 0/5 1What is the primary reason to put an AI gateway between your app and the model providers, once you use more than two? Frontier models are cheaper through a gateway than directGateways make virtual keys, budgets, fallbacks, and unified logging one implementation instead of N per providerGateways speed up token generation by more than 20% 2You point Claude Code at a LiteLLM proxy with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. What must ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN be? The Anthropic root API key, forwarded as-isThe proxy's master key (admin credential)A virtual key issued by the proxy, scoped to allowed models with its own budget 3OpenRouter's fallback array promotes to the next model when the first one fails. Which of these DOES it trigger on? Only network 5xx errors5xx errors, rate limits, downtime, context-length errors, AND content-moderation refusalsOnly rate limits (429) 4You need to install LiteLLM in production. Which versions are safe post the March 2026 incident? Any version, PyPI has cleaned everythingv1.82.6 and earlier, OR v1.83.0 and later (v1.82.7 and v1.82.8 are compromised)Only versions after v2.0.0 5You're a solo dev on Vercel who wants to try Claude, GPT, and Gemini in one afternoon. Best fit? Self-hosted LiteLLM with Postgres and RedisVercel AI Gateway or OpenRouter — hosted, one key, zero infraRoll your own aggregator with LangChain AI gateways at a glance flipTermAI gateway (definition)DefinitionMiddleware between your app and the model providers. One request shape, N providers behind it, plus virtual keys, budgets, fallback, logging, and caching.Press Enter or Space to flip the card. Use the left and right arrow keys to move between cards.Term shown. ←Prev 1 / 9 Next→ Key takeaways An AI gateway is the missing router between your app and every model — it exists to make virtual keys, budgets, fallback, logging, and caching a single implementation instead of N per provider Pick on TWO axes first: self-hosted vs. hosted (LiteLLM/Portkey OSS vs. OpenRouter/Vercel), and minimalist vs. control-panel (OpenRouter/Vercel vs. LiteLLM/Portkey) The Claude Code killer workflow: point ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL at your own LiteLLM proxy and issue per-developer virtual keys — team gets shared limits, logs, and one-click revoke without touching the root Anthropic key OpenRouter's models[] array is the shortest path to silent Claude → GPT → Gemini fallback, but note that moderation refusals are a fallback trigger too — review the list like an ACL After the March 2026 LiteLLM supply-chain attack, pin to v1.82.6 or earlier, or v1.83.0+; prefer the signed Docker image over pip; egress-allowlist the proxy A gateway is transport, not product — prompt portability and evals still need real work, no matter how many models you can now reach

Intermediate At WWDC 2026 (announced 8 June 2026) Apple shipped the third generation of its Foundation Models — AFM 3 — and expanded the Foundation Models framework in a way that matters even if you never write Swift: the framework now takes third-party LLM providers (Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini are shipping as Swift packages), and the on-device path stops being a toy 3B model and adds a 20-billion-parameter sparse MoE that runs on Apple Silicon by keeping most experts in NAND and swapping only what a prompt needs into RAM. If you build Claude apps and have been treating "on-device" as a separate universe from your API workflows, that gap is closing this year. This page unpacks what actually shipped, the non-obvious mechanisms, and the concrete migration and compatibility choices you now have. What you'll learn Name the four AFM 3 models — Core (3B), Core Advanced (20B sparse), Cloud, Cloud Pro — and which one runs where Understand the flash-plus-DRAM expert-routing trick that lets a 20B model fit on an iPhone at all Use the Foundation Models framework's @Generable / @Guide macros for constrained decoding — the model literally cannot emit invalid JSON Know what changed at WWDC26: the LanguageModel / LanguageModelExecutor protocols that let you plug Claude or any other LLM into the same Swift session API Decide when to reach for the on-device 3B, when to jump to Private Cloud Compute, and when to keep the workload on the Claude API Last verified: 2026-08-09. This page quotes facts that change over time — treat the date above as its freshness. Confirm against the official source.
documents.s: Apple Foundation Models 3 & the On-Device LLM Stack for Claude Users

documents.t: AFM 3 is Apple's second serious swing at on-device LLMs: a rebuilt 3B dense model (Core), a new 20B sparse MoE (Core Advanced) that runs on iPhone by keeping most experts in flash storage, a Cloud and Cloud Pro pair on Apple Silicon plus NVIDIA GPUs in Google Cloud, and a framework that now treats Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini as first-class swappable providers behind the same LanguageModel protocol. Free for developers to call on-device; free on Private Cloud Compute for App Store Small Business Program members under 2M first-time downloads.
Everyone is writing the "Apple has a 3B on-device model" headline. Here are the mechanisms most write-ups skip.

The naive read of "20-billion-parameter model on iPhone" is impossible: even at 4-bit, 20B weights is ~10 GB, well past what an iPhone can hold in RAM. Apple's trick, per the WWDC 2026 announcement, is to store the full AFM 3 Core Advanced model in flash memory (NAND) and swap only the input-dependent routed experts into DRAM at inference time. The architecture has shared experts that stay resident and routed experts that a router picks per prompt (activating 1–4B parameters at a time, not the full 20B). Combined with Quantization Aware Training, this is what lets Apple ship a 20B-class model on a device that has ~8 GB of usable RAM. The consequence for you: iPhone-side latency is now dominated less by matrix multiply and more by NAND read bandwidth and the router's choices — a very different performance envelope than a 3B dense model.
documents.s: 1. The 20B model fits on iPhone because most of it lives in NAND, not RAM

documents.t: The framework's @Generable macro is often described as "structured output," which understates what it does. @Generable runs at compile time: it generates a JSON schema and a parser for your Swift type, and the framework then uses that schema for constrained decoding — the on-device model is forced, at the token level, to produce output that parses back into your Swift struct. There is no "hope it's valid JSON, then retry." A @Guide annotation lets you add constraints (.anyOf(["PG", "PG-13", "R", "G"]), ranges, descriptions) that are also enforced at decode time. If you have spent time writing JSON-repair fallbacks around a Claude tool-use loop, the on-device 3B model side of your app can drop that entire retry layer.
documents.s: 2. Constrained decoding is baked into the Swift compiler, not the runtime

documents.t: The WWDC 2026 session "Bring an LLM provider to the Foundation Models framework" shipped two new protocols: LanguageModel (declares capabilities and executor configuration) and LanguageModelExecutor (handles the actual generation, KV cache, and streaming). Anyone can ship a Swift package that conforms to them — Apple explicitly named Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini as launch-time providers. The consequence: from the app's point of view, the same LanguageModelSession, the same @Generable types, the same tool-calling contract, and the same transcript model apply whether the underlying model is the on-device 3B, Private Cloud Compute, Claude on Anthropic's API, Gemini on Google Cloud, or an MLX weights file from Hugging Face. Model choice becomes a Swift package dependency rather than an SDK rewrite.
documents.s: 3. The framework now takes any LLM — including Claude and Gemini — behind one Swift API

documents.t: flipTermAFM 3 CoreDefinition3B-parameter dense on-device model. Rebuilt from the second-generation 3B, natively multimodal (text + image + audio), 25 languages. Runs on all Apple Intelligence–capable devices. Free for on-device calls.Press Enter or Space to flip the card. Use the left and right arrow keys to move between cards.Term shown. ←Prev 1 / 6 Next→

Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1AFM 3 Core (3B) — always on-device⌄ Runs on any Apple Intelligence device. Free to call from Swift via the Foundation Models framework — no API key, no network, no per-token bill. This is where you put classification, extraction, summarization, on-device rewrites, and anything that must work in airplane mode. ←PreviousNext→ 2AFM 3 Core Advanced (20B) — newer iPhones only⌄ Runs on Apple's most powerful silicon; older Apple Intelligence devices transparently fall back to Core. Use this when the 3B refuses or hallucinates on a task and the request can wait for expert-swap latency but must stay on-device (e.g. private health/finance reasoning). ←PreviousNext→ 3AFM 3 Cloud / Cloud Pro — Private Cloud Compute⌄ The framework routes to PCC when the device model isn't enough. You do not choose the specific server SKU — you request a reasoning level and Apple picks. Same privacy contract as on-device: PCC's node attestation prevents Apple staff from reading your requests. ←PreviousNext→ 4Third-party providers — via Swift package⌄ Add a package that conforms to LanguageModel + LanguageModelExecutor (Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini are the launch-time examples). From the session API the code is identical — model choice is a package dependency. ←PreviousNext→

The framework's headline feature is that you can get typed, schema-validated output from the on-device 3B with almost no ceremony. On-device 3B call with @Generable structured output (Swift) CopyOpen in Claude↗ import FoundationModels @Generable struct TripIdea { @Guide(description: "Short, evocative title") let title: String @Guide(description: "One-paragraph pitch, 40–80 words") let summary: String @Guide(.range(1...14)) let estimatedDays: Int @Guide(.anyOf(["easy", "moderate", "hard"])) let difficulty: String } let session = LanguageModelSession() // defaults to on-device Core let idea = try await session.respond( to: "Suggest a shoulder-season trip in Puglia for a family with a 6-year-old.", generating: TripIdea.self // constrained decoding ) print(idea.title, idea.difficulty, idea.estimatedDays) At runtime the model is forced, at the token level, to emit tokens that keep the running text parseable as a TripIdea. You never see a JSON string; you receive a TripIdea value. This is the same contract whether the session is talking to the on-device 3B, PCC, or a third-party provider you plumbed in as a Swift package.

The WWDC 2026 "Bring an LLM provider" session made this concrete: implement LanguageModel and LanguageModelExecutor, publish it as a git-tagged Swift package, and app code that already used the on-device 3B can call your provider by changing one initializer. Sketch of a third-party provider conforming to LanguageModel CopyOpen in Claude↗ import FoundationModels public struct ClaudeSonnet5: LanguageModel { public let capabilities = LanguageModelCapabilities(capabilities: [ .toolCalling, .guidedGeneration, .reasoning ]) public var executorConfiguration: ClaudeExecutor.Configuration } public final class ClaudeExecutor: LanguageModelExecutor { public struct Configuration: Hashable { // hashable = KV-cache key public var modelID: String public var tokenProvider: TokenProvider // NOT a plain API key string } public required init(configuration: Configuration) throws { /* … */ } public func respond( to request: LanguageModelExecutorGenerationRequest, model: Model, streamingInto channel: LanguageModelExecutorGenerationChannel ) async throws { // 1. Map Foundation Models transcript → Anthropic /messages payload // 2. Stream deltas back via channel.send(.response(action: .appendText(...))) // 3. Surface tool calls / reasoning via the same transcript entry types } } Two subtleties the API deliberately pushes you toward. First, Configuration is Hashable on purpose: the framework caches executors by configuration, so same config = same executor = preserved KV cache across turns. Second, the guidance explicitly discourages plain API-key strings in initializers — prefer a TokenProvider or a sign-in flow, keychain-persist tokens, and use App Attest for cloud calls to verify the device isn't a tampered build hitting your endpoint from the outside.
documents.s: Bringing Claude into the same Swift session

documents.t: Pro tip Reach for on-device AFM 3 Core (3B): summarization, classification, entity extraction, on-device rewrites, keyboard suggestions — anything where a bounded prompt and typed output beats a network round-trip. Free. Reach for AFM 3 Core Advanced (20B): private reasoning that cannot leave the device (health, finance, unreleased documents) and that the 3B fumbles. Expect variable latency because of NAND expert-swap. Reach for Private Cloud Compute (Cloud / Cloud Pro): larger context, longer reasoning, or multimodal where the 20B on-device can't keep up but privacy still rules out third-party APIs. Stay on Claude via the Anthropic API (or the new Swift-package provider): long agent runs, extended thinking, big-context codebase work, and cross-platform apps that need the same model on Android and web. See the Claude vs others foundations page. Do NOT wrap the on-device 3B in a JSON-repair loop: it has constrained decoding. If your output isn't parsing, the schema is wrong or you skipped @Generable.
documents.s: When to use what — a decision table for Claude builders

documents.t: On-device is the counterweight to the local-agent story we cover in Local AI agents and Run models locally with Ollama. Apple's angle is different: it is first-party OS integration, not a separate local server. If you are picking between Apple's on-device model and running Claude alongside it, the design patterns are in Claude + local models: hybrid patterns and Local or Claude agent. For a broader framing of "how do these models differ and which do I pick," see Choosing a model and Porting prompts across models. Security implications of shipping a local + cloud hybrid live in Securing local and hybrid agents.

Check yourself 0/5 1How does AFM 3 Core Advanced fit a 20B-parameter model onto an iPhone? It runs a shrunk-and-distilled 3B version and calls it 20B for marketingIt stores full weights in NAND flash and swaps only input-dependent routed experts into DRAM, activating 1–4B parameters per promptIt streams every token from Private Cloud Compute and caches locallyIt uses a new 1-bit quantization that shrinks the model to fit RAM 2What does the @Generable macro give you that hand-rolled JSON prompting does not? A retry loop that auto-fixes malformed JSONA prettier print of the model's raw outputCompile-time schema generation plus token-level constrained decoding, so the output is guaranteed to parse into your Swift typeA speed boost by avoiding the tokenizer 3You want to call Claude Sonnet 5 from an iOS app that already uses the Foundation Models framework for on-device summarization. What is the WWDC26-native path? Rewrite the app around the Anthropic SDK — the framework only supports Apple modelsAdd a Swift package that conforms to LanguageModel + LanguageModelExecutor, then swap the session's model in one lineProxy every Claude call through Private Cloud ComputeConvert Claude's weights to a Core ML package and ship them in the app bundle 4Which developer group gets Private Cloud Compute calls for free from the framework? Every free-tier Apple Developer Program accountApp Store Small Business Program members with under 2 million first-time downloadsOnly Apple's own first-party appsAnyone with an Enterprise Developer Program membership 5Why is the executor `Configuration` type required to be `Hashable`? So it can be sent across Swift concurrency boundariesSo the framework can cache executors by configuration — same config keeps the KV cache warm across turnsTo satisfy the compile-time schema generatorBecause Swift 6 requires all protocol types to be Hashable

Gemini for Claude Users

Advanced On September 22, 2026, Unreal Labs released Unreal Agent — an MIT-licensed agent harness written in Go — and published benchmark runs showing it matching Codex's pass rate on Terminal-Bench 4.0 for $1,428 against $2,350. Same model, same tasks, same score, 39% less money. The interesting part is not the number. It is where the money went. Unreal Agent's central claim is that a large slice of what you pay a coding agent is not reasoning at all — it is the model sitting in the loop managing its own waiting. This page is about that mechanism, because it transfers to any harness you build or buy, including ones that have nothing to do with Unreal Labs. What you'll learn Understand the async tool-call event flow: what gets appended to the session log, when, and what the model actually sees Learn why turn count — not output length — is the unit that drives agent cost, and how to measure it in your own loop Read the published cost table honestly: what the dollar figures cover and what they do not Know the three designs Unreal Labs deliberately refused to build (sub-agents, workflows, harness-level security hooks) and the argument for each Apply the transferable rules to your own agent, whichever harness you already use Last verified: 2026-09-23. Benchmark figures, architecture and design rationale are from Unreal Labs' launch post and repository, published September 22, 2026. All benchmark runs are the vendor's own, executed with GPT-6 Astra at xhigh reasoning; no independent replication existed at the time of writing. The repository showed roughly 1.4k stars the day after launch. Confirm against the official source.
documents.s: Async-First Agent Harnesses: What Unreal Agent Changes

documents.t: Unreal Agent is an MIT-licensed Go harness that appends every tool call to an append-only session log as an in-progress event and lets execution continue in the background, so the model never blocks and never polls — which cuts turns, and turns are what you actually pay for.

Here is a normal synchronous agent turn: Model emits a tool call. Harness runs the tool. The loop is suspended. Tool returns. Harness appends the result. Harness calls the model again with the full transcript. Now the same turn in Unreal Agent: Model emits a tool call. Harness immediately appends an event to the session log saying the call is in progress, and starts execution in the background. Execution continues. The model is free to issue more calls. When the tool completes, its result is appended to the log — and that append is what triggers the next model call. The model sees the running state and then the final result, in order, in its own transcript. It never has to encode "wait for this", never issues a poll, never carries heartbeat bookkeeping in its reasoning. Unreal Labs' framing: the harness lets the model "issue more heavy tool calls per model turn without wasting tokens on polling or waiting for them." That is the whole idea. It is small. It is also the part most harnesses get wrong, because a synchronous loop is the obvious thing to write.

Every model turn re-sends the accumulated transcript. A 30-turn agent run does not cost 30× a single call — it costs roughly the sum of a growing context across 30 calls. Turn count is therefore closer to a quadratic cost driver than a linear one, and it dominates anything you save by trimming the system prompt. Look at what the published runs report alongside the dollars: Benchmark Pass rate Unreal Agent Turns Codex Pi Pi turns Terminal-Bench 4.0 57.9% $1,428 28 $2,350 $1,827 44 SWE-Atlas Codebase QnA 65.8% $936 16 $1,303 $1,033 — DeepSWE 1.1 72.4% $1,367 26 $1,633 $1,584 — ALE-CLI 30.0% full pass $217 — — — — On Terminal-Bench 4.0 the comparison is 28 turns versus Pi's 44 — a 36% reduction in turns for a 22% reduction in cost against Pi, and 39% against Codex. The turn column is the causal one; the dollar column is the consequence. This is the same lesson AILmanac covers from the other direction in why agents burn tokens: the expensive thing in an agent is not the answer, it is the re-reading. Pro tip Instrument turn count before you instrument anything else. If you only log tokens, you will optimise prompts and miss the loop. A useful diagnostic: count how many of your agent's turns produced no tool call and no user-visible output. Those are pure loop overhead — waiting, checking, re-planning — and they are what an async harness removes. Parallel-capable tools amplify the effect. If your three slowest tools can run concurrently, a synchronous loop pays for all three serially in wall-clock AND in turns.
documents.s: Why this shows up as money

documents.t: The rationale matters more than the code, because these are arguments you can apply to whatever harness you already run.
documents.s: Three things they deliberately did not build

documents.t: Unreal Labs chose "a straightforward asynchronous tool-calling model" over sub-agent delegation and predefined workflows. The reasoning is that once tool calls are genuinely async, most of what sub-agents were for — running things in parallel without stalling the parent — is already handled by the loop. Sub-agents then add context-splitting, result-merging and their own turn overhead for a problem you no longer have. This is a real position, not the only one. Multi-agent designs still win where you genuinely want isolated context, not just parallelism. But "we need sub-agents to do two things at once" is a claim worth re-testing against an async loop first.

This is the sharpest argument in the launch post, and it is worth quoting the shape of it: security and approvals that rely on harness hooks "tend to require more maintenance and be less robust than deterministic environment or sandbox constraints, outside the harness." What they recommend instead: allowed and disallowed hosts, granular access tokens, and proxies with approval gates. In other words, put the control where the agent physically cannot reach it. The logic is straightforward once stated. A harness hook is code running in the same process as the agent loop, gating a tool the agent can already invoke. A sandbox boundary is enforced by the kernel or the network, below the agent entirely. If your agent has a bash tool — and Unreal Agent's does — an in-process allowlist is a speed bump, not a wall. AILmanac's securing local and hybrid agents covers how to build the outer boundary.

Unreal Labs moved away from vendor SDKs (Anthropic's Agent SDK is named) because those assume "local sessions, subprocesses, and resource limits that don't translate neatly into production use." That is a deployment-shape argument, not a quality one. An SDK modelled on a local CLI session assumes one process, one machine, one lifetime. A production agent fleet wants sessions that outlive a process and can be resumed on a different box — which is exactly what Unreal Agent's append-only, versioned session store provides, including forking a session to branch a run. If you are building a product on top of an agent loop, this is the question to ask of any SDK: can a session survive the process that created it?

The harness is deliberately small and explicitly composable — eight replaceable components behind documented interfaces: Session inbox — deduplicates inputs. Every input carries a globally unique, stable caller ID, so retries do not double-apply. Coordinator — owns LLM turns and dispatches operations. Session store — append-only persisted history, supports forking, versioned. Context builder — assembles the model input. Performs no I/O. LLM adapter — talks to the provider. Tool registry and translators — validate calls synchronously and must "perform no I/O or suspend the loop". Operation manager — runs the durable background work. Two constraints in that list do the heavy lifting and are easy to miss: the context builder and tool translators are forbidden from doing I/O. That is what keeps the coordinator's hot path deterministic and non-blocking — all latency is pushed into operations, which are the things designed to be async. If you build your own harness, this is the rule to steal. Storage formats and operations are versioned, and an unsupported session version errors explicitly on resume rather than half-loading. That is the correct failure mode for durable state, and it is rarer than it should be. The built-in tool surface is three tools: Bash, ViewImage, and Skill-use — the last of which hooks into the portable skill format AILmanac covers in SKILL.md as an open standard. Three tools is the point: a small, token-cheap tool surface is part of the cost story.

Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Install⌄ Go 1.27+ toolchain, then go install the runner from the cmd/ path, or clone and use the bundled Makefile (make build, make test). ←PreviousNext→ 2Pick a provider⌄ Selected by environment variable. OpenAI, OpenAI Codex, OpenRouter, Fireworks and Ollama are supported, so you can point the same harness at a hosted frontier model or a local one. ←PreviousNext→ 3Run a single prompt⌄ The runner takes -p for a prompt and -workspace for the directory the agent works in, in the same shape as claude -p. Output is a JSONL transcript you can redirect to a file. ←PreviousNext→ 4Read the transcript, not the summary⌄ The JSONL run log is where the async event flow is visible: in-progress events, then results. Counting the model-call events in it gives you the turn count that drives your bill. ←PreviousNext→ 5Put the boundary outside⌄ Before you point it at anything real, set the sandbox: restricted filesystem, allowlisted hosts, scoped tokens. The harness deliberately does not do this for you. ←PreviousNext→ Install and run (from Unreal Labs' documented usage) CopyOpen in Claude↗ go install github.com/unreallabsai/unreal-agent/cmd/unreal-agent-runner@latest export OPENAI_API_KEY="..." unreal-agent-runner -p 'Inspect this project and explain how to run its tests.' Point it at a different provider and keep the transcript CopyOpen in Claude↗ export UNREAL_HARNESS_LLM_PROVIDER=openrouter export UNREAL_HARNESS_LLM_MODEL=<model-id> unreal-agent-runner \ -workspace ./my-project \ -p 'Summarize this project.' > run.jsonl

Four caveats, because the numbers are good enough that they deserve scrutiny: Every run is the vendor's own. No third party had replicated them at the time of writing. One model. All published runs used GPT-6 Astra at xhigh reasoning. The async advantage should generalise — it is a loop property, not a model property — but "should" is not "was measured". The dollars are whole-suite totals, not per-task costs. They are comparable to each other and not to your workload. Pass rates are matched, not improved. The claim is explicitly same score, less money. On DeepSWE 1.1 Unreal Agent reports 72.4% at $1,367 against Codex's $1,633 — a 19% saving, notably smaller than the 39% on Terminal-Bench. The advantage scales with how tool-heavy and how long-running your tasks are. On short tasks with few tool calls, expect close to nothing. That last point is the practical one. If your agent does three tool calls and finishes, async buys you almost nothing. If it does sixty over half an hour, it buys you the difference between the two columns.

You do not have to adopt Unreal Agent to use any of this: Measure turns. It is the cost variable most teams do not log. Make slow tools non-blocking, even if your harness is otherwise synchronous. Returning a handle immediately and delivering the result as a later event is a change you can make inside most loops. Keep the hot path I/O-free. Context assembly and tool-call validation should never wait on the network. Move approvals out of the process. Network policy, scoped credentials and a gating proxy beat an in-process allowlist that lives next to a bash tool. Shrink the tool surface. Three good tools cost fewer tokens per turn than fifteen mediocre ones, on every single turn. Check yourself 0/5 1In Unreal Agent, what happens the instant the model emits a tool call? The loop suspends until the tool returnsAn in-progress event is appended to the session log and execution continues in the backgroundThe call is queued until the end of the turnA sub-agent is spawned to own the call 2Why does cutting turn count save more money than cutting output length in an agent loop? Output tokens are cheaper than input tokensEach turn re-sends the accumulated transcript, so cost grows faster than linearly with turnsProviders charge a fixed fee per turnTurns are billed at the reasoning-token rate 3Why does Unreal Labs argue against implementing approvals as harness hooks? Hooks are slower than native callsHooks run in the same process as an agent that already has a bash tool, so a sandbox or network boundary is the more robust controlHooks are not supported in GoHooks break session forking 4The context builder and tool translators are forbidden from performing I/O. What does that constraint buy? Smaller binary sizeCompatibility with more providersA deterministic, non-blocking hot path — all latency is pushed into operations, which are the components designed to be asyncLower token usage per call 5On which kind of workload should you expect the async advantage to be smallest? Long autonomous sessions with many slow tool callsShort tasks that finish in a handful of tool callsTasks that read large codebasesTasks that run tools in parallel flipTermUnreal Agent — what and whenDefinitionSeptember 22, 2026. Unreal Labs. MIT-licensed async-first agent harness in Go (module github.com/unreallabsai/unreal-agent, Go 1.27+). Ships as a library, a runner executable, and a Harbor-compatible benchmark runner. ~1.4k stars the day after launch.Press Enter or Space to flip the card. Use the left and right arrow keys to move between cards.Term shown. ←Prev 1 / 8 Next→ Key takeaways Turn count, not token count, is the cost variable in an agent loop. Instrument it first. Making tool calls non-blocking removes polling and waiting turns — 28 turns vs 44 for the same Terminal-Bench 4.0 pass rate is the whole argument. The advantage is proportional to tool-heaviness: 39% on Terminal-Bench, 19% on DeepSWE, ~0 on a three-call task. Security belongs outside the harness. An in-process approval hook next to a bash tool is a speed bump; a sandbox and a gating proxy are a boundary. Keep context assembly and tool validation I/O-free. Push every wait into a durable operation. All published numbers are vendor runs on one model. Treat them as a well-argued hypothesis about your workload, not a measurement of it.

Intermediate For most of 2025 the practical answer to "how does my coding agent drive the web?" was Playwright or Puppeteer wrapped in a tool. That works for scripted flows but breaks on the interesting cases — anything behind a login, anything that needs a real Chrome profile, anything you'd rather not re-authenticate on every run. A newer pattern has emerged in mid-2026: a shared-login browser that runs alongside your own tabs, hands each agent its own isolated workspace, and gives you back structured page snapshots instead of raw HTML. On July 24, 2026 the reference implementation — citrolabs/ego-lite — hit #1 on GitHub Trending, and every major agent CLI (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Kiro) got support the same week. This page is the practical read on that pattern: what it fixes that headless-browser tools don't, how it plugs into Claude Code specifically, and the security trade-off you're signing up for the moment you let an agent share your Google session. What you'll learn Understand what a 'shared-login browser for agents' is and why it beats headless Playwright for the interesting cases See how Spaces isolate agent tabs from your own without launching separate profiles Learn what a semantic snapshot returns (and why it uses fewer tokens than a DOM dump) Install ego lite and its skill into Claude Code with two commands Weigh the real security cost of handing an agent your logged-in cookies — and know what NOT to do
documents.s: Shared-Login Browsers for AI Agents: The ego lite Pattern

documents.t: Every agent that has ever tried to browse the web has hit the same three walls: Login walls. Anything behind SSO — GitHub, your email, your project tracker, your bank — is invisible to a fresh Playwright profile. Storing credentials in an agent config to work around this is a security fire. DOM dumps blow the token budget. A Google Docs page or a modern React app snapshots into tens of thousands of tokens of noise. Most of it is layout scaffolding the model doesn't need. Your Chrome and the agent's Chrome are fighting for the same window. Kick off a long browsing task and either you can't use your browser for 20 minutes, or the agent's tabs interfere with your work. ego lite's approach — and the reason the same pattern is now spreading — is to treat these as one problem. Run a single custom Chromium build. Give the user their own tabs. Give every agent its own Space — an isolated workspace with its own tab stack but sharing the profile. Emit semantic snapshots instead of raw DOM. Everything stays local; no separate profile management, no shipped-off HTML.

From the ego lite documentation: "Spaces are workspaces both you and your agent can use. Group your tabs by project in yours; your agent runs tasks on its own." The important detail is what a Space is not — it is not a separate browser profile and not a separate cookie jar. It is a partitioned tab surface sharing the same underlying session. That's what makes shared-login work: when the agent's Space navigates to github.com, it inherits the same auth cookies your logged-in tabs use, without the agent needing to see or store your credentials. The isolation is at the UX and tab-management layer, not the security boundary. This is the load-bearing distinction most reviewers miss. It's why the pattern is practical (agents just work on your logged-in sites) and it's also why the security section below matters (an agent operating in a Space has the same effective privileges as you). Watch out The Space model shares session cookies by design. That is the whole point — and the whole risk. Anything a compromised or prompt-injected agent can do in its Space, it can do as you, on any site you're logged into. Treat "give my agent a Space" as equivalent to "let my agent act as me on the web" — because it is.
documents.s: Spaces: how the isolation actually works

documents.t: The other shift is what the agent reads when it "looks at" a page. Playwright hands you a DOM. ego lite hands the model a semantic snapshot — a structured summary of the page's interactive elements with stable references you can act on, produced from inside a custom Chromium engine rather than a JavaScript shim on stock Chrome. The vendor claim is that "complex browser tasks finish up to 3.45x faster than agent-browser, on fewer tokens" (lite.ego.app). The exact multiplier depends on the task; the direction — fewer tokens, more reliable ref actions across iframes and shadow DOM — is the durable insight, and it's the same reason Chrome DevTools' Accessibility Tree and the emerging W3C AI-oriented DOM proposals lean the same way. ★ Why this matters beyond ego lite: the "give the model a semantic view, not a DOM dump" idea is going to spread. When you evaluate any browser-for-agents tool in the next 12 months, ask what shape the snapshot has. If it's an HTML dump, you're paying for it in every turn's token count. If it's a structured, refable snapshot, the agent can plan on it cheaply.

Two artifacts, two commands. First the browser app (a Chromium build for macOS — Windows and Linux are on the roadmap but not shipping as of late July 2026), then the skill that teaches your agents to talk to it. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Install the browser⌄ Download the .dmg from the project site (Apple Silicon or Intel), or install via the project's documented flow. First launch offers optional migration of Chrome logins, cookies, extensions, and bookmarks into the ego lite profile. ←PreviousNext→ 2Add the ego-browser skill to your agent⌄ In your terminal: npx skills add citrolabs/ego-lite — this installs the skill globally so every agent on your machine that supports skills (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Kiro) discovers it. ←PreviousNext→ 3Verify from inside Claude Code⌄ Start Claude Code and type /ego-browser — the skill should appear in the completion list. If it doesn't, restart the CLI so the skill registry is re-scanned. ←PreviousNext→ 4Try one task in plain language⌄ In Claude Code: /ego-browser open my GitHub notifications and summarize the ones from the last 24 hours. The agent picks up the ego-browser skill, opens a new Space, reads a snapshot, acts on the page, and reports back — your own tabs untouched. ←PreviousNext→ 5Watch the first run⌄ Look at what the agent clicks and what data comes back to it in the snapshot. This is your calibration for what to trust it with next. ←PreviousNext→ Claude Code — start small: agent runs a single authenticated task in its own Space CopyOpen in Claude↗ /ego-browser Open my GitHub notifications tab. For each notification from the last 24 hours, report: repo, kind (issue/PR/mention), title, and a one-line summary of the newest comment. Do not click through, do not mark anything as read, do not navigate away from the notifications page. Notice what the prompt does: it defines the surface (notifications page), the read-only scope (report; don't click; don't mark), and the artifact (a structured list). Every prompt you give a shared-login agent should have those three elements, because you are running it as yourself.
documents.s: Installing ego lite for Claude Code

documents.t: The skill exposes a small set of JavaScript-callable tools the agent writes snippets against — navigate, snapshot, click, fill, wait, capture. The code-based approach is deliberate: instead of a chatty tool-calling loop where the agent asks "please click element ref-12," the agent writes a JavaScript block that composes several actions and receives one structured result back. That's where the "fewer turns, fewer tokens" claim comes from in practice — the round-trip count drops. You don't need to write those snippets yourself. The skill and the model do. What you should know is: Every action is referenced against the last snapshot. If the page changed underneath the agent, the ref is stale and the tool errors — an important self-correcting property. The skill includes an install.md in skills/ego-browser/references/ — a good place to read if your agent complains it can't find the browser. The MIT-licensed source lives under citrolabs/ego-lite at roughly 4.3k stars as of late July 2026, and the same repo hosts the ego-browser skill sources. Last verified: 2026-07-26. ego lite is shipping fast. The install command (npx skills add citrolabs/ego-lite), the macOS-only status, the exact skill functions, and the 3.45x claim all reflect the state of the project on July 26, 2026 — check the repo README and the project site for the current version, supported OSes, and any changes to the skill surface. Confirm against the official source.
documents.s: What's actually in the ego-browser skill

documents.t: This is where most of the enthusiastic tweets stop and where the interesting engineering starts. Handing an agent a Space that inherits your logged-in sessions is functionally equivalent to giving it your session cookies. Everything the same-origin policy would allow you to do in a browser — post on your behalf, exfiltrate documents from Google Drive, transfer money from a banking session, invite an outside collaborator to a private repo — is inside the agent's ability. That's not a bug in ego lite; it's the value proposition. The security posture is the price of the ergonomics. Three concrete practices reduce the blast radius without giving up the win: Different Spaces for different trust tiers. Personal Google + email in one Space. Work SaaS in another. Anything experimental or untrusted (arbitrary URLs from the internet) in a third that has been logged out of everything that matters. Never point a shared-login agent at an untrusted URL you didn't fetch. The whole class of indirect prompt-injection attacks lands hardest here — a page can carry hidden instructions that steer the agent into a data-exfiltration action against your other logged-in sites. Related: Agentic browsers and same-origin risk. Read-only prompts by default. Ask for summaries and lists first. Introduce actions (clicks, form fills) only after you have seen the snapshot the agent is reasoning over. This is the same discipline that makes autonomous runs safe.
documents.s: The security cost you are signing up for

documents.t: Grok, Cursor, and Kiro have all added shared-browser integrations in the same month, and the underlying mechanism — a custom Chromium plus a skill layer that emits semantic snapshots — is likely to be standardized rather than owned by any one project. The interesting near-term question is not whether every coding agent gets a shared-browser mode; it's whether the snapshot format converges (so an agent skill written for one browser works on another) or fragments the way early MCP servers did. The concept to hold onto: the browser is becoming a shared surface between humans and agents, not two separate browsers pointed at the same pages. That reshapes what "computer use" costs and what it can safely be pointed at. See also Computer-use agents for how Claude's own browser-control feature compares to this pattern, and Cloudflare Kitesurf for the stateless end of the same spectrum — a browser runtime built for automation rather than shared-login, where the trade is 3-7x less CPU/memory at ~1.7x more wall-clock time. Check yourself 0/4 1What is a Space in ego lite? A separate Chrome profile with its own cookie jarA partitioned tab surface sharing the same underlying browser session and profileA remote sandbox on citrolabs' servers 2Why does a semantic snapshot beat a raw DOM dump for agent work? It's encrypted end-to-endIt compresses to fewer tokens and gives stable refs for actions across iframes and shadow DOMIt's rendered as an image the model can see 3What is the primary security risk of a shared-login browser agent? The browser uploads your history to citrolabs' serversData leaves your machine only when you sync bookmarksThe agent can act as you on any site your Space is logged into — including as the target of indirect prompt injection from untrusted pages 4You want to try ego lite for the first time with Claude Code. What's the safest first prompt? Open my banking dashboard and pay this invoiceOpen my GitHub notifications and summarize the last 24 hours — read only, don't click throughBrowse to any URL I give you and take whatever actions seem useful Key takeaways Shared-login browsers give agents their own Space in your real browser session — solving login walls, DOM-dump token cost, and window contention in one design. ego lite ships this pattern for macOS today; the ego-browser skill (npx skills add citrolabs/ego-lite) makes it available to Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Kiro. Semantic snapshots cut per-turn tokens and give stable action refs; the exact multiplier varies, the direction is the durable insight. The security cost is real: an agent in a shared Space has your privileges on every site you're logged into. Use separate Spaces by trust tier, keep untrusted URLs out, prefer read-only prompts first. This is a pattern, not a product. Expect convergence on 'browser as shared surface between humans and agents' across the ecosystem in the next 6–12 months.

Beginner You already think in Claude. Now a teammate shares a Custom GPT, or a client lives in ChatGPT, and you need to be productive there today — without relearning how to use an AI assistant from scratch. Good news: almost everything you know transfers. This page maps your Claude mental model onto ChatGPT, flags the handful of things that genuinely work differently, and tells you when each one tends to shine. What you'll learn Translate Claude concepts to their ChatGPT equivalents (Projects, Custom GPTs, custom instructions/memory, canvas, the model picker) Know which of your Claude prompting habits carry over unchanged (most of them) Spot the few things you genuinely have to adjust Know when to reach for ChatGPT vs when to stay in Claude Last verified: 2026-06-28. Exact model names, the layout of the model picker, plan tiers, file/upload limits, prices, and which features pair with which model change constantly at OpenAI. This page teaches the durable mental model and concept-mapping; for any specific name, limit, or price, check OpenAI's own current docs (linked in Sources) rather than trusting a number here. Confirm against the official source.

If you only read one section, read this. Here's how the things you know in Claude line up with ChatGPT: In Claude you call it… In ChatGPT it's… Same idea? Claude Projects (workspace + files + project instructions) Projects Yes — nearly the same concept Custom Style / a saved system prompt you reuse Custom GPTs (a packaged, reusable assistant) Close, with a twist (see below) Your account-level preferences / "how I want you to respond" Custom instructions Yes Claude's memory of past chats Memory Yes — same idea, evolves often Artifacts (side panel for documents/code) Canvas Yes — same idea Model selector (Opus / Sonnet / Haiku) The model picker (speed vs reasoning tiers) Yes — same idea, different names Tool use / function calling (API) Function calling Yes — same shape, different JSON details The takeaway: there's almost no new concept to learn. It's mostly renaming and relocating things you already understand.

This is the single point where Claude users most often get confused, because ChatGPT has two things that both feel like "a customized Claude," and they're for different jobs. Projects are organizational — a workspace that bundles many chats, uploaded files, and shared instructions around one ongoing effort. Continuity across multiple conversations is the point. Reach for a Project when you'd open a Claude Project: a long research thread, an evolving piece of writing, a workstream with reference docs. Last verified: 2026-06-28. OpenAI describes Projects as workspaces that group chats, files, and custom instructions; availability across free and paid plans changes over time — check the current help page. Confirm against the official source. Custom GPTs are packaged assistants — a saved configuration (a system prompt, optional knowledge files, enabled tools, sometimes API actions) that you invoke as a single, fresh chat with a fixed persona. They're built to be reused and shared, so one person builds the expertise and many people run it. Last verified: 2026-06-28. Custom GPTs bundle instructions, optional knowledge files, and tools into a reusable assistant; configuration options and limits change — verify on OpenAI's current docs. Confirm against the official source. The mental shortcut: Need continuity across many chats with shared context? → Project. Need a reusable, shareable specialist that behaves the same every time? → Custom GPT. A subtle gotcha for Claude users: a Custom GPT chat tends to start fresh each time with only its preset instructions plus that conversation — don't expect it to remember your last session the way an ongoing Project thread does.
documents.s: Projects vs Custom GPTs — the one distinction worth getting right

documents.t: In Claude you set global preferences and let it remember context. ChatGPT does the same, just with more explicit layers you can set instructions at: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Account-level custom instructions⌄ Your standing preferences — tone, detail level, what to focus on. Applied to all chats, like your Claude account preferences. ←PreviousNext→ 2Project instructions⌄ Context scoped to one Project's subject — the equivalent of Claude Project instructions. ←PreviousNext→ 3Custom GPT instructions⌄ The 'system prompt' baked into a packaged assistant. This is where a builder fully controls behavior. ←PreviousNext→ 4In-chat, one-off⌄ Just say it in the conversation when you need a single-message adjustment — exactly like Claude. ←PreviousNext→ Memory is its own evolving system: ChatGPT can carry context across separate chats. Treat what it remembers, how much, and where it's available (e.g. inside Custom GPTs or not) as volatile — it changes frequently, so verify current behavior rather than assuming. Last verified: 2026-06-28. Custom instructions apply across chats and can be layered at user, project, and GPT level; specifics and availability change — check the current help article. Confirm against the official source.
documents.s: Custom instructions & memory — same idea, slightly different layers

documents.t: If you love Claude Artifacts — a side panel where a document or code block becomes a live, editable object — you'll feel at home with canvas. It opens a dedicated editing surface for writing and coding so you and the model can revise in place instead of regenerating the whole message. Same instinct, different name. One thing to watch (and a good example of why we don't hard-code specifics): which models support canvas can change, and not every model is paired with it. If canvas doesn't appear, it may be the selected model — switch models or check the current docs rather than assuming it's broken. Last verified: 2026-06-28. Canvas is a side-panel editing interface for writing and coding; model compatibility and availability change over time — verify on OpenAI's current help page. Confirm against the official source.

Just as you choose Opus vs Sonnet vs Haiku, ChatGPT asks you to pick a model — generally along a speed ↔ reasoning spectrum (fast/instant options for quick turns, higher-reasoning options for hard problems, with the top tiers gated to paid plans). The names and number of tiers shift often; the durable skill is the same one you already use with Claude: match the model to the task's difficulty and your latency/cost tolerance. This is exactly the framework in Choosing a Model and Which Claude Should I Use? — it's provider-agnostic. Don't memorize a model name; learn to read "fast vs deep" and pick accordingly. Pro tip Reach for the fast/instant tier for routine drafting, formatting, and quick Q&A. Reach for the high-reasoning tier for multi-step logic, tricky code, or careful analysis. If a feature like canvas or a tool seems missing, suspect the selected model before you suspect a bug.
documents.s: The model picker — pick by job, not by name

documents.t: If you've done tool use with Claude, OpenAI's function calling will feel immediately familiar, because the loop is the same: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Declare tools⌄ You describe each tool with a name, a description, and a JSON-schema of its parameters (which are required, their types). Same idea as a Claude tool definition. ←PreviousNext→ 2Model requests a call⌄ Given the prompt and the available tools, the model returns a structured tool call — the tool name plus arguments — instead of (or alongside) text. ←PreviousNext→ 3You execute it⌄ Your application runs the actual function with those arguments. The model never runs anything itself. ←PreviousNext→ 4Return the result⌄ You feed the tool's output back to the model. ←PreviousNext→ 5Model answers⌄ It uses the result to produce the final response — and may request more calls before finishing. ←PreviousNext→ What's identical: the describe → model-requests → you-execute → return-result → answer loop, multiple/parallel calls, and the principle that the model proposes, your code disposes. Last verified: 2026-06-28. OpenAI function calling defines tools via JSON schema (name, description, parameters) and follows a request → tool-call → execute → submit-result → response loop; exact field names and options change — check the current API guide. Confirm against the official source. What differs and will trip you up if you copy-paste: the exact JSON field names, how tool calls and results are represented in the message list, "strict"/structured-output options, and the specific API endpoint shape. As a rule across providers, prompting and architecture transfer; wire-format details do not — always re-check the per-provider schema.
documents.s: Function calling — same shape, different JSON details

documents.t: Your hard-won Claude habits are not wasted. These carry over essentially unchanged: Prompt structure — clear role, explicit task, examples, requested output format → Prompting Basics Giving context deliberately — paste the right material, scope it, don't dump everything Asking for a specific output format — tables, JSON, steps; works the same Iterating in place — refine via follow-ups (and now via canvas) The tool-use loop — describe tools, let the model call them, return results → Tool Use Choosing a model by task difficulty — fast vs deep, same judgment call Provider-neutral system prompt — drop into a Custom GPT or a Project's instructions CopyOpen in Claude↗ You are a {role}. Goal: {one clear sentence}. Rules: - Use ONLY the context I provide; if the answer isn't there, say "I don't know". - Be concise. No preamble. - Output format: {exact format — e.g. a markdown table with columns X, Y, Z}. When you need information you don't have, ask one focused question instead of guessing.

A short, honest list of things that are actually different: Two "customization" objects, not one. Decide up front: ongoing workspace (Project) or reusable assistant (Custom GPT)? Picking the wrong one is the most common early mistake. Feature ↔ model pairing. In ChatGPT, whether canvas (or a given tool) is available can depend on the selected model. When something's missing, check the model first. Wire-format for tools. The function-calling concept is identical; the JSON details are not — never reuse Claude's exact tool JSON verbatim. Volatile specifics. Model names, tiers, limits, and prices move fast. Build the habit of confirming at the source, exactly as you should for Claude too.

Both are excellent general assistants and the gap on any given task is often small and shifting — so treat this as tendencies, not laws, and let your own eval on your own data decide: Reach for ChatGPT when you need its specific ecosystem — a Custom GPT a team already maintains, a Project a collaborator set up, or a built-in tool/integration you rely on there. If your client or coworkers live in ChatGPT, meeting them there beats friction. Reach for Claude when you're already in the Claude workflow this site is built around — Projects, Artifacts, and the prompting/agent patterns documented throughout AILmanac — and want to go deep on them. The honest answer most of the time: whichever you (or your team) are already set up in. The skill is portable; the setup cost is the real switching cost. Use the left and right arrow keys to move between cards.Term shown. ←Prev 1 / 6 Next→ Check yourself 0/3 1You want a workspace that keeps many related chats, reference files, and shared instructions together for an ongoing research effort. What do you use in ChatGPT? A Custom GPTA ProjectCustom instructions 2You've used Claude tool use. What's true about OpenAI function calling? A completely different concept you must relearnThe same describe→call→execute→return loop, but the exact JSON field names differIdentical down to the JSON, so you can paste Claude's tool definitions unchanged 3Canvas doesn't appear when you expect it. What's the most likely first thing to check? Your internet connectionWhether the selected model supports canvasWhether you've used up your memory Key takeaways There's almost no new concept — Projects ≈ Claude Projects, Custom GPTs ≈ a packaged reusable assistant, canvas ≈ Artifacts, function calling ≈ tool use. Get the one distinction right: Projects = organize many chats; Custom GPTs = a reusable, shareable specialist. Your prompting, context, output-format, and tool-loop habits transfer unchanged — choose models by task difficulty, same as Opus/Sonnet/Haiku. Adjust only a few things: two customization objects, feature↔model pairing, and tool-call JSON details. Names, tiers, limits, and prices go stale fast — verify specifics at OpenAI's docs, just as you should for Claude.

Beginner AILmanac's core is Claude — but the skills travel. The same prompting, context-engineering, tool-use and eval habits work on almost any modern model. This page widens the lens to the whole field: who the major players are, how to choose for a task, and what carries over no matter which you use. What you'll learn Know the major AI assistants & models and what archetype each one is Use a repeatable framework to pick a model for a specific task — not by hype See which skills transfer across every model (most of them) Know which facts go stale fast — and where to check the current truth Last verified: 2026-06-28. Model names, versions, context limits, prices and benchmark rankings change almost monthly — treat any specific number as perishable. This page teaches the durable parts (archetypes + how to choose); for today's specifics check each provider's own model page (linked in Sources) or an independent tracker like Artificial Analysis. Confirm against the official source.
documents.s: The AI Model Landscape: Choosing Among Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini & Open Models

documents.t: Think in archetypes — the rankings shuffle, the archetypes are stable: Anthropic — Claude · frontier closed model. Known for coding, agentic/tool use, long-context reasoning, and a safety-first posture. (The whole rest of this site goes deep here.) OpenAI — ChatGPT / GPT · frontier closed model with the largest consumer ecosystem and a very broad, multimodal feature set. Google — Gemini · frontier closed model, deeply wired into Google's products and data, with very large context windows. Meta — Llama · open-weight: you can download and self-host it. The backbone of much of the local/open ecosystem. Mistral · open-weight + API, European, efficiency-focused. xAI — Grok · closed, integrated with X, leaning on real-time signal. DeepSeek / Qwen (Alibaba) · strong open-weight models known for capability-per-cost; popular for self-hosting. Pro tip The biggest practical fork is CLOSED frontier (best raw capability, hosted only) vs OPEN-WEIGHT (self-hostable, private, customizable, often cheaper to run at scale). Don't shop by leaderboard. The only benchmark that matters is YOUR task on YOUR data.
documents.s: The major players (by archetype, not ranking)

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Write down the task + the hard constraints⌄ What must it do, and what's non-negotiable: data privacy (can data leave your network?), budget, latency, max context, regulated domain, on-device requirement. ←PreviousNext→ 2Closed-frontier or open-weight?⌄ Need the absolute top capability with zero infra? A closed frontier model (Claude / GPT / Gemini). Need privacy, self-hosting, heavy customization, or lowest run-cost at scale? An open-weight model (Llama / Mistral / Qwen / DeepSeek) you host. ←PreviousNext→ 3Shortlist 2-3 candidates⌄ Pick a couple that plausibly fit the constraints — don't agonize; you'll test them. ←PreviousNext→ 4Build a tiny eval on YOUR data⌄ 10-50 real cases with known-good answers. Run each candidate. This beats every public leaderboard for your use case. ←PreviousNext→ 5Weigh cost & latency at your real volume⌄ Multiply per-call cost and speed by your expected traffic. The 'best' model can be the wrong one if it's 10x the price for a 2% quality gain you don't need. ←PreviousNext→ 6Pick — and keep the eval⌄ Re-run it when a new model drops. Switching is cheap when you have an eval; it's a coin-flip when you don't. ←PreviousNext→ Provider-neutral system prompt skeleton (works on any model) CopyOpen in Claude↗ You are a {role}. Goal: {one sentence}. Rules: - Use ONLY the provided context; if the answer isn't there, say "I don't know". - Output: {exact format / schema}. Context: {context} Task: {task}
