Advanced On 17 September 2026, PrismML published Ternary Bonsai 2 27B: a 27-billion-parameter model whose weights are only -1, 0 and +1, packed into a 5.95 GB file, released Apache 2.0. The Hugging Face GGUF repo passed 2.5 million downloads inside five days. The headline everywhere was the same — a 27B model that fits on a laptop. The headline is true. Almost everything people assume follows from it is not. Stock llama.cpp will load the file and produce fluent nonsense without raising an error. Ollama and LM Studio refuse it outright. The 5.95 GB file needs roughly 12 GB of VRAM at default settings. The larger 7.21 GB build is faster on a datacenter GPU and slower on a 4090. And the widely-quoted "98.2% of full precision" is an average across fourteen benchmarks that hides a 6-point collapse in multimodal reasoning and, in one independent test, complete failure on low-resource languages. This page is the practical layer: what ternary quantization actually buys you, how to run this model without silently corrupting your output, and how to read a compression retention number honestly. The technique outlives the model — the same reasoning applies to every low-bit release that follows. What you'll learn Understand why ternary weights are 1.75 bits in practice, not the 1.58 bits the theory promises Recognise the silent-garbage failure mode: stock loaders ignore the Hadamard rotation and never error Pick between PTQ1_0 and PQ2_0 using the bandwidth-vs-unpack crossover, not file size Budget real memory: 5.95 GB of weights, ~64 KiB per token of cache, and why defaults blow past 12 GB Read '98.2% retention' correctly — which capabilities survive compression and which quietly do not
documents.s: Ternary Quantization in Practice: Bonsai 2 27B in 5.95 GB

documents.t: A normal model stores each weight as a 16-bit float. A ternary model stores each weight as one of three values — -1, 0, +1 — with a single shared FP16 scale per group of weights. Reconstruction is w = scale_g * t, where t is the trit. Three states need log₂(3) ≈ 1.58 bits. That is the number the research literature uses, from Microsoft's BitNet b1.58 onward. It is not the number you get on disk. Bonsai 2 27B ships at 1.75 bits per weight for its densest build. The extra 0.17 bits per weight is the part nobody explains: Group scales. One FP16 scale per group of 128 weights is 16 bits amortised over 128 weights — 0.125 bits per weight before anything else. Packing waste. Trits do not divide neatly into bytes. Dense packing recovers most but not all of the theoretical density. Unquantized components. Embeddings, output projections and normalisation layers stay at higher precision. On a 27B model these are a small fraction of parameters but a noticeable fraction of bytes. So the real ratio is not 16/1.58 ≈ 10×. It is 53.8 GB → 5.95 GB, or about 9× — which is exactly what the model card reports. :::tip Why ternary is fast, and it is not the maths The intuition most people have is that ternary multiplication is cheap: multiplying by -1, 0 or +1 is a sign flip, a skip, or nothing. True, but that is not where the win comes from on real hardware. Token generation is memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound. Every generated token requires streaming the entire weight matrix from memory. Cut the bytes by 9× and you cut the dominant cost by 9×. The arithmetic was never the bottleneck. This matters practically: a CPU or GPU without native ternary support must dequantize back to a normal format to use its existing multiply-accumulate units, which throws away the arithmetic saving while keeping the bandwidth one. Which is why the packing format you pick changes performance in a direction that looks backwards — see below. :::

This is the single most important thing on this page, and it appears in almost no coverage of the release. Bonsai 2's weights have a blockwise Hadamard rotation folded into storage. A matching inverse transform must be applied to the activations at runtime. The rotation is a standard trick for low-bit quantization — it spreads outlier magnitudes across a block so the ternary grid has less to lose — but it means the stored weights are not directly usable by a loader that does not know about it. A stock llama.cpp build does not know about it. Depending on version it will either reject the tensor types or, worse, load the file successfully and generate fluent, confident, completely wrong output. There is no error, no warning, no degraded-quality flag. The model card states this plainly: stock llama.cpp will not run these files, and standard builds produce garbage because the Hadamard activation transform is missing. Downstream tools inherit the problem in different ways: Runtime Behaviour with Bonsai 2 27B GGUF PrismML's llama.cpp fork (branch prism) Works — the only local GGUF path today Stock llama.cpp Rejects the tensor types, or loads and emits nonsense Ollama Import fails with a tensor size overflow error LM Studio Rejects ggml tensor types 142 and 143 MLX (Apple) Separate mlx-2bit build required; larger footprint The Ollama and LM Studio failures are the safe outcome. The stock-llama.cpp silent success is the dangerous one, because a benchmark script or an eval harness will happily record the nonsense as a result. :::warning If you are evaluating a low-bit model, verify the loader first Run one known-answer prompt before you run anything else. If a model that scores 95+ on HumanEval cannot answer "what is 2+2" coherently, you have a loader problem, not a model problem. This applies to every exotic quantization format, not just this one. :::
documents.s: The trap: stock llama.cpp loads it and lies

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Build PrismML's fork, not mainline⌄ git clone https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp && cd llama.cpp, then cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON && cmake --build build -j for NVIDIA. On Apple Silicon drop the CUDA flag — Metal is on by default. On AMD use -DGGML_HIP=ON. The default branch is prism; the README explicitly warns against building from prism-v6 and against mixing this fork's libraries with a stock llama.cpp install on the same machine. ←PreviousNext→ 2Pick the right GGUF before downloading 7 GB⌄ PTQ1_0 is 5.95 GB at 1.75 bits per weight — dense trits. PQ2_0 is 7.21 GB at 2.13 bits per weight — each trit gets its own 2-bit slot. Same weights, same quality, different packing. The choice is a throughput decision, not a quality one. See the crossover table below. ←PreviousNext→ 3Download, and check the byte count⌄ hf download prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf --local-dir . — PTQ1_0 is 5,946,648,928 bytes and PQ2_0 is 7,206,168,928 bytes. A truncated download is another way to get plausible-looking garbage. Add the mmproj file (629 MB at Q8_0, 931 MB at BF16) only if you need vision. ←PreviousNext→ 4Serve it with an explicit context size⌄ ./build/bin/llama-server -m Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf --alias bonsai-2-27b -ngl 99 -fa on -c 32768 --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080. The -c flag is not optional in practice: -c 0 defaults to the full 262K window and will try to allocate roughly 16 GB of attention cache before it has generated a single token. ←PreviousNext→ 5Verify with a known-answer call, then wire up your tooling⌄ The server exposes an OpenAI-shaped /v1/chat/completions endpoint, so anything that speaks chat-completions can point at http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1. Send one trivial prompt and read the answer with your own eyes before you point an eval harness or an agent loop at it. ←PreviousNext→ 6If PQ2_0 crashes on CPU, disable repacking⌄ PQ2_0 can crash during llama.cpp's CPU repack step. Pass --no-repack, or set LLAMA_ARG_REPACK=0 in the environment. ←PreviousNext→ Minimal end-to-end: build, fetch, serve, verify CopyOpen in Claude↗ # 1. Fork only — stock llama.cpp will silently produce garbage git clone https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/llama.cpp && cd llama.cpp cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON && cmake --build build -j # 2. Fetch (PQ2_0 = 7.21 GB, faster on big GPUs; PTQ1_0 = 5.95 GB, fits 8 GB cards) hf download prism-ml/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf \ Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf --local-dir . # 3. Serve — always set -c explicitly, never leave it at 0 ./build/bin/llama-server -m Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PQ2_0.gguf \ --alias bonsai-2-27b -ngl 99 -fa on -c 32768 \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 # 4. Verify the loader BEFORE trusting any output curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"model":"bonsai-2-27b","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is 2+2? Answer with one number."}]}' # Coherent "4" => loader is correct. Fluent nonsense => wrong build, stop here.

Two builds of the same weights. PTQ1_0 packs trits densely at 1.75 bits. PQ2_0 gives each trit its own 2-bit slot at 2.13 bits — 21% more disk, but the unpacking is far cheaper because slots are byte-aligned. Measured generation throughput, tokens per second: GPU PQ2_0 (7.21 GB) PTQ1_0 (5.95 GB) Winner RTX 5090 129.9 120.5 PQ2_0 RTX 4090 81.2 91.1 PTQ1_0 L4 (24 GB) 29.8 32.1 PTQ1_0 M5 Pro (Metal) 28.1 — — The pattern generalises: PTQ1_0 wins on Ada-generation and lower-end GPUs, PQ2_0 wins on H100, A100 and Blackwell. That is the opposite of the usual quantization rule of thumb, where smaller is always faster. The reason is the bandwidth-versus-unpack tradeoff from earlier. On a bandwidth-starved card, moving 21% fewer bytes dominates and the dense packing wins. On a card with enormous memory bandwidth, bandwidth stops being the constraint and the bit-shuffling cost of dense unpacking becomes the bottleneck instead — so the fatter, byte-aligned format runs faster. Prompt processing tells the same story more loudly: on an RTX 5090, PQ2_0 processes prompts at 3,893 tok/s against PTQ1_0's 1,805 — more than double, because prefill is compute-bound, where unpacking cost hits hardest. Rule of thumb: below 12 GB of VRAM you have no choice, take PTQ1_0. Above it, take PQ2_0 unless you are on a 4090 or an L4, where PTQ1_0 measurably wins.
documents.s: PTQ1_0 vs PQ2_0: the crossover that looks backwards

documents.t: Three different "size" numbers are circulating for this model — 5.9 GB, 7.2 GB and 8.6 GB — and all three are defensible, because they measure different things. Here is the actual budget: Weights: 5.95 GB (PTQ1_0) or 7.21 GB (PQ2_0). Vision projector: +629 MB (Q8_0) or +931 MB (BF16), if you need images. Attention cache: roughly 64 KiB per token. That is ~0.5 GB at 8K context, ~2 GB at 32K, and ~16 GB at the full 262K window. Parallel slots: llama.cpp allocates cache per slot. Defaults allocate several. One independent test measured just over 12 GB of VRAM at default settings, dropping to about 8 GB when the server was restricted to a single parallel slot. The disk footprint they measured — around 7 GB — corresponds to the PQ2_0 build, which is where part of the number confusion comes from. Practical context headroom by card, using PQ2_0 unless noted: VRAM Build Usable context 8 GB PTQ1_0 ~16K tokens (~6K with vision) 12 GB PQ2_0 ~56K tokens 16 GB PQ2_0 ~118K tokens 24 GB PQ2_0 ~240K tokens 32 GB+ PQ2_0 Full 262K window The "runs on a laptop" claim survives all of this — but "runs on a laptop with an 8 GB GPU and a 16K context" is the honest version, and that is a materially different product.
documents.s: File size is not memory requirement

documents.t: PrismML reports an aggregate of 84.78 against the full-precision base model's 86.32 across fourteen benchmarks — the 98.2% figure. Averages are where compression damage goes to hide. The per-benchmark spread: Benchmark Bonsai 2 27B FP16 base Delta AIME26 95.83 94.58 +1.25 MATH-500 98.80 99.80 −1.00 LiveCodeBench 90.07 90.05 +0.02 HumanEval+ 95.12 93.29 +1.83 MMLU-Redux 89.09 91.46 −2.37 MMMU-Pro 75.49 81.73 −6.24 Three things to take from this table. First, the damage is not uniform — it is structural. Maths and code are essentially untouched. Knowledge recall drops (composite knowledge-and-reasoning lands near 79.9 versus 85.6 for full precision). Multimodal reasoning takes the real hit: MMMU-Pro falls 6.24 points, and OCR Bench v2 drops from 60.99 to 56.88. Compression costs you breadth of stored fact, not procedural skill — which is exactly what you would expect when you crush the precision available to store long-tail associations. Second, be suspicious of the positives. The compressed model "beating" its own full-precision base by 1.83 points on HumanEval+ and 1.25 on AIME26 is not evidence that compression helps. It is evidence that these benchmarks have run-to-run variance of a couple of points. Which should also make you discount the small negatives. Third, the vendor's own numbers do not fully agree. The model card's benchmark table aggregates to 84.78, while PrismML's launch post reports an aggregate of 83.9. Both are described as the same 98.2% retention. The discrepancy is small and unexplained; we report it rather than pick one. :::danger The failure mode benchmarks did not catch One independent hands-on test found behaviour no benchmark row predicts: asked to translate into low-resource languages including Tamil, the model entered a repetitive loop and never completed the task — worse than the previous Bonsai generation. The same test found it identified a real timezone bug and then talked itself out of the correct conclusion, and failed to produce a working reset button in a small HTML task across three correction rounds. This is the characteristic signature of aggressive quantization: aggregate scores hold, while the long tail — rare languages, long-horizon self-correction — degrades in ways that only show up in use. Community reports also describe recall and coherence degradation past roughly 200K tokens of the advertised 262K window. :::

There is a parallel effort to get ternary Bonsai into upstream llama.cpp, and its current state is a useful lesson in how low-bit formats fragment. PrismML proposed group-128 ternary packing for the smaller Bonsai models. The llama.cpp maintainer pushed back in favour of group size 64, on the grounds that it costs under 6% extra memory while supporting more tensor shapes and giving better quality. Q2_0 with group-64 became the official format and has been merged into multiple backends including CUDA and Vulkan. PrismML kept their group-128 variants in the fork. So "does llama.cpp support ternary models" has two correct and opposite answers: Yes — Q2_0_g64 builds run on mainline across backends, and the fork's own README points at them as the portable path. No, not for this model — as of verification, the published Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf repo contains F16, PQ2_0, PTQ1_0 and the two mmproj files. There is no Q2_0_g64 build of the 27B. The fork is the only path. Two older ternary formats, TQ1_0 and TQ2_0, already exist in ggml but use group size 256, which is incompatible with how these models are natively packed. TQ2_0 is also the tightest faithful ternary layout in ggml at roughly 2.06 bits per weight — and in current mainline it implements a CPU-only dot product with no CUDA, Metal or Vulkan path. Seeing "ternary supported" in a changelog tells you very little about whether your GPU will use it. For the next low-bit model you evaluate, the question to ask is not is it quantized but which group size, which packing, which backends have kernels, and is there a portable build — because that determines whether you are running on mainline or maintaining someone else's fork.
documents.s: The mainline story, and why it matters for the next release

documents.t: Worth it when: You need a capable maths or coding model on hardware that cannot hold a 27B at higher precision. That is where retention is near-perfect and the value is highest. You are bandwidth-constrained — a laptop GPU, an edge box, a shared L4 — and 9× fewer bytes per token is the difference between usable and not. Energy matters. PrismML reports 0.714 mWh per token on an RTX 4090, which they put at 40% more efficient than a full-precision 8B model. The Apache 2.0 licence and fully local execution are requirements, not preferences. Not worth it when: The work is knowledge-heavy or multimodal. That is precisely where the compression bill lands. You need non-English long-tail language coverage. The independent evidence here is bad and benchmarks did not predict it. You cannot maintain a forked inference runtime. Ollama and LM Studio do not load it today, and a stock build fails silently rather than loudly. You were going to run it past ~200K tokens of context on the strength of the 262K spec. flipTermWhat is Bonsai 2 27B, precisely?DefinitionA ternary-quantized compression of Qwen3.8-27B (27.36B parameters) published by PrismML on 17 September 2026 under Apache 2.0. Architecture unchanged from the base model; only the weight representation differs.Press Enter or Space to flip the card. Use the left and right arrow keys to move between cards.Term shown. ←Prev 1 / 10 Next→

documents.t: Check yourself 0/5 1You download Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-PTQ1_0.gguf, run it on a recent stock llama.cpp build, and it generates fluent text that is subtly wrong. What is the most likely cause? The download was corruptedStock llama.cpp does not apply the required Hadamard activation transform, so it loads the file and produces garbage without erroringThe temperature is too highThe model needs a system prompt 2You have an RTX 4090 with 24 GB. Which GGUF build gives higher generation throughput? PQ2_0 — it is larger so it must be higher qualityPTQ1_0 — 91.1 tok/s vs PQ2_0's 81.2 on that cardThey are identical; the files only differ in disk sizeNeither runs on a 4090 3Your card has 8 GB of VRAM. The weights file is 5.95 GB. You launch llama-server with default settings and it runs out of memory. Why? The file is secretly larger than advertisedAttention cache costs roughly 64 KiB per token and llama.cpp allocates it per parallel slot — defaults push total usage past 12 GBTernary models require double the VRAM of their file size by designThe vision projector is always loaded 4A teammate cites '98.2% of full-precision performance' to argue the compressed model is a drop-in replacement for a document-understanding pipeline. What is the strongest objection? 98.2% is within benchmark noise so the number is meaninglessRetention is highly uneven — maths and code are at parity while MMMU-Pro drops 6.24 points and OCR Bench v2 falls from 60.99 to 56.88, which is exactly the workload in questionThe model is not licensed for commercial use27B models are never suitable for document understanding 5A changelog says llama.cpp 'supports ternary quantization'. What must you still check before assuming your GPU will use it? Nothing — ternary support is a single feature flagGroup size, packing format, and which backends have kernels — TQ2_0 is CPU-only in mainline, and the Bonsai 2 27B repo ships no Q2_0_g64 buildOnly whether the file is under 8 GBWhether the model is Apache 2.0 licensed Last verified: 2026-09-22. Intermediate "How much does AI cost?" has no single answer — it depends on which pricing archetype you're buying and how much you actually use it. The dollar figures churn every few months; the structure of the cost barely moves. This page teaches the durable shape: the three ways AI is priced, how to estimate a workload before you build it, the levers that cut the bill, and the real fork between renting an API and self-hosting. What you'll learn Tell apart the three cost archetypes: per-token API, flat subscription, and open/self-hosted Estimate any workload's cost from tokens × rate × volume — before you ship it Pull the big levers that cut spend without hurting quality Know when open/self-hosted beats API on cost, and when API wins Know which numbers go stale fast — and where to check today's truth Last verified: 2026-06-28. Per-token rates, subscription tiers, cache and batch discounts, and which model is cheapest change almost monthly — treat every specific dollar figure as perishable. This page teaches the durable model (archetypes + how to estimate + the levers); for today's numbers check each provider's own pricing page (linked in Sources), an independent tracker like Artificial Analysis, and run the math in our Cost Calculator. Confirm against the official source.

Almost every way you can pay for AI collapses into one of three shapes. Learn the shapes, not the prices. Per-token API (usage-based). You call a hosted model over an API and pay per token — and input and output are priced separately, with output almost always the more expensive of the two. Bigger/smarter models cost more per token; smaller models cost far less. Most providers also offer discounts: a reduced rate for cached input you re-send, and a flat batch discount for non-urgent async jobs. This is how you pay when you build a product on Claude, GPT, or Gemini. Cost scales directly with usage — pennies at small scale, the dominant line item at large scale. Flat consumer/seat subscription. A fixed monthly fee for a chat app or IDE assistant (the Claude / ChatGPT / Gemini consumer plans, Copilot-style seats). You don't see tokens; you get a usage allowance and rate limits. Predictable and cheap for a human at a keyboard — but it doesn't scale to programmatic/high-volume work, and per-seat costs add up across a team. Open / local (self-hosted). You run an open-weight model (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek) on your own hardware or a rented GPU. There's no per-call price — you pay for the hardware (or hourly GPU rental) + electricity + ops, whether the model is busy or idle. The marginal cost of one more call is effectively near-zero at scale, but you carry fixed cost and operational burden. See Run Models Locally with Ollama. Pro tip The key split: API and subscriptions are MARGINAL cost (you pay per use); self-hosting is mostly FIXED cost (you pay to keep capacity up, used or not). On the API, the single biggest surprise is that OUTPUT tokens usually cost several times more than input — verbose answers cost real money. A flat subscription is the right tool for a human chatting; the per-token API is the right tool for an app calling the model in a loop.

You can size an API bill before writing a line of production code. The whole model is one formula: cost ≈ (input tokens × input rate) + (output tokens × output rate), per call × number of calls Rates are quoted per million tokens, and input and output have different rates — so estimate the two halves separately and add them. A rough token rule of thumb: ~1 token ≈ 4 characters of English, or ~0.75 words. For exact counts, use the Token Estimator area and read Tokens & Pricing. The full mechanics of where tokens hide live in The Token Economy. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Size ONE call's tokens⌄ Add up the input: system prompt + tools + retrieved context + history + the user turn. Then estimate the output you ask for. Count input and output separately — they're priced differently. ←PreviousNext→ 2Multiply each side by its own rate⌄ input tokens × input rate, plus output tokens × output rate. Use today's per-million numbers from the provider's pricing page (don't trust a figure you memorized — see VerifyNote). ←PreviousNext→ 3Scale by real volume⌄ Multiply the per-call cost by calls per day × days. A cost that's trivial per call (fractions of a cent) becomes your top line item at millions of calls — model your ACTUAL traffic, not one request. ←PreviousNext→ 4Apply the discounts you'll actually use⌄ If a big chunk of input repeats every call, price it at the CACHED rate, not full input. If the job is offline, apply the BATCH discount. These change the answer dramatically at scale. ←PreviousNext→ 5Sanity-check against a tracker, then cut⌄ Compare your per-token assumptions to an independent tracker and our Cost Calculator, then attack the bill with the levers below. ←PreviousNext→ Back-of-envelope estimate (fill in today's rates) CopyOpen in Claude↗ Per call: input_tokens = system + tools + context + history + user_turn output_tokens = the answer you ask for call_cost = (input_tokens * input_rate_per_million / 1e6) + (output_tokens * output_rate_per_million / 1e6) Per month: monthly_cost = call_cost * calls_per_day * 30 Then adjust: - cached repeated input -> use the (lower) cache-read rate for that slice - offline / non-urgent -> apply the batch discount to the whole job Rates change monthly — pull today's numbers from the provider's pricing page.

documents.t: Most real workloads carry dead weight. These levers, roughly in order of leverage, cut spend without touching quality — pull the cheap structural ones first. Right-size the model. Don't pay a flagship rate for a job a small/cheap model does fine. Classification, extraction, routing, and simple formatting usually run great on the smallest tier at a fraction of the per-token price. Reserve the big model for genuinely hard reasoning, and consider routing: cheap model handles the easy majority, escalate only the hard cases. See Choosing a Model. Trim the context you send. The cheapest token is the one you never send. Prune bloated system prompts, compact long histories into a running summary, and expose only the tools the task needs — every one is input you re-pay each call. RAG instead of stuffing huge context. Pasting a 50-page document to answer one question pays for 50 pages every call. Retrieval fetches only the few relevant passages — far fewer input tokens for the same (often better) answer. Reach for a giant context window only when you genuinely need the whole corpus in view at once. Prompt caching. If many calls share a large unchanging prefix (system prompt, tool catalog, reference doc), caching processes it once and re-serves it at a steep discount on every later call. The single highest-leverage structural change for chat and agent workloads, because it pays back every turn. Batch the non-urgent. Evals, bulk labeling, summarizing an archive — anything where you don't need the answer in seconds — runs through an async batch path at a flat discount on most providers. Trade immediacy for a materially lower bill. Shorten the output. Output is the pricier side. Ask for JSON or a tight schema instead of a chatty paragraph: fewer output tokens and no downstream parsing guesswork. Smaller / open models for the easy slice. For the high-volume, low-difficulty majority of calls, an open or small model can be dramatically cheaper per call — sometimes near-free if you already self-host. Keep the frontier model for the cases that actually need it. Pro tip These stack multiplicatively: cached input × right-sized model × terser output × batch discount compounds into a large total cut on an easy task — with quality unchanged. Pull the structural levers (right-size, cache, RAG, batch) before micro-optimizing wording — they move the bill far more. Always MEASURE the change against the real bill, not a guess. The deep playbook is The Token Economy.
documents.s: The big levers to cut cost

documents.t: This is the decision that actually moves your AI budget. It's a fixed-vs-marginal-cost crossover, and volume is the variable that decides it. Open / self-hosted wins at HIGH, steady volume. Once you're running enough calls to keep a GPU busy most of the time, the near-zero marginal cost per call beats paying per token forever. You amortize the fixed hardware/rental cost across a huge number of calls, gain data privacy and full customization — and accept the operational burden (provisioning, scaling, uptime, MLOps) as the price of admission. API wins at LOW or SPIKY volume, or with no infra. If traffic is small, bursty, or unpredictable, paying per token means you pay only for what you use and nothing when idle — no GPU sitting warm at 3 a.m. You also skip all the ops. For most teams shipping a product, prototyping, or with traffic that comes in spikes, the API is both cheaper and far less work. Watch out Self-hosting is rarely 'free.' The model weights may be free, but GPUs, electricity, and the engineer-hours to keep it running are not — count them honestly before claiming a saving. Idle GPUs are pure loss: fixed-cost infra only beats per-token pricing when utilization is HIGH. Low or spiky traffic favors the API every time. The crossover point moves whenever API prices drop or hardware gets cheaper — re-run the math periodically, don't decide once and forget. Estimate before you build: (input × input rate) + (output × output rate), per call × volume — then apply cache and batch discounts. Biggest levers: right-size the model, trim context, RAG over huge context, prompt caching, batch the non-urgent, shorten output. Self-hosting wins at HIGH steady volume (amortize fixed cost); API wins at LOW/spiky volume or with no infra (pay only for use). Every dollar figure goes stale fast — verify at the provider's pricing page and a tracker, and run your own numbers in the Cost Calculator.

Intermediate A chat turn costs a fraction of a cent. The same question handed to an agent — one that reads files, calls tools, and loops until done — can cost dollars. Teams are discovering this the hard way: a coding agent left running racks up a bill that a human at a keyboard never would. The scary part isn't the average; it's that you can't predict it in advance, and the cost of the same task can swing wildly. This page explains why agents burn tokens (the mechanism is not what most people guess), shows the numbers that surprise even experienced builders, and gives you the four levers that actually cut the bill — the same levers whether you're on Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or a home-grown loop over any model. What you'll learn Explain the context snowball — why agent cost grows roughly QUADRATICALLY with steps, not linearly Cite the real multipliers: agentic tasks ~1000x a chat's tokens, and the SAME task varying up to 30x Know when a second agent is worth it — and the benchmark showing it usually isn't Pull the four cost levers that work: budget caps, prompt caching, model-tier routing, context pruning Diagnose a runaway agent bill and put a hard ceiling on it Last verified: 2026-07-15. Per-token prices, per-developer monthly spend, and which model is cheapest change almost monthly — treat every dollar figure here as perishable and illustrative. The mechanism (context snowball, re-read tax) and the levers are durable; the exact ratios come from 2026 benchmarks and research linked in Sources. Confirm today's rates on each provider's pricing page before quoting a bill to anyone. Confirm against the official source.
documents.s: Why AI Agents Burn Tokens (and How to Cap the Bill)

documents.t: Here's the trap. A chat is one turn — one input, one output, done. An agent is a loop: it reads a task, takes an action, reads the result, takes the next action, and so on until the job is finished. The catch is that on every step, the model re-reads the entire accumulated conversation so far — the original prompt, every prior action, and every tool result — before deciding what to do next. So the input grows on every step, and you pay for the whole snowball again each time it rolls forward: Step 1 processes the prompt. Step 2 re-reads the prompt + step 1's action + result. Step 3 re-reads all of that + step 2's action + result. …and so on. Add up the input across a run and the total scales roughly with the square of the number of steps, not linearly. The Stanford Digital Economy Lab found agentic tasks to be "uniquely expensive, consuming 1000x more tokens than code reasoning and code chat" — and crucially, it's the input tokens that dominate, not the output. The agent isn't writing more; it's re-reading more. What you'll learn The cost driver is re-reading, not thinking. Each loop step re-processes the full transcript, so a 20-step run pays for early context ~20 times over. This is why 'just let the agent figure it out' is expensive: every extra step it takes multiplies against everything before it. Output-heavy tasks (write me an essay) are cheap by comparison; input-heavy loops (explore this repo, then fix the bug) are where the money goes.
documents.s: The context snowball: why cost grows quadratically

documents.t: Three figures reset most people's intuition: ~1000x. Agentic tasks can consume roughly a thousand times the tokens of an equivalent chat or code-completion, per the Stanford analysis — driven by the snowball above, not by a bigger model. Up to 30x variance on the same task. The same agent, run on the same task, can cost up to 30x more one time than another — because the path it takes (how many tools it calls, how far it wanders) is non-deterministic. You genuinely cannot know the bill until it's done. This is why "result-based pricing" for agents is so hard: you only see the cost after everything runs. More agents rarely pay for themselves. 2026 production benchmarks found that a multi-agent setup added only ~2.1% accuracy at 2x the cost versus a well-configured single agent on 64% of tasks. A hierarchical-supervisor pattern pushed a document task from 85% → 95% accuracy — but at roughly $0.15/task vs $0.003 for the single agent (~50x). More agents buys a little accuracy for a lot of money. Watch out Because the same task varies up to 30x, an average-based budget WILL be blown by the tail. Cap the ceiling, don't budget the mean. Adding agents to 'be safe' usually multiplies cost far faster than it adds accuracy. Reach for a second agent only when the task genuinely decomposes into parallel, independent subtasks.

Before the loop even starts, how the agent reaches its tools sets a floor on cost. Connecting a set of MCP servers can inject tens of thousands of tokens of tool definitions into every step of the snowball. A rough comparison many builders hit: a plain CLI command averages ~200 tokens, while the equivalent MCP operation can cost 32k–82k tokens once tool schemas and wrapping are counted. That gap rides along on every loop step. That doesn't make MCP wrong — it's the right choice for auth, multi-tenancy, and governed access. It means the tool surface is a cost lever you chose at design time. AILmanac has a dedicated deep-dive: The MCP Token Tax covers Tool Search, deferred loading, and code execution as the three fixes.
documents.s: Your tool surface is part of the bill

documents.t: Optimization advice is endless; only four levers move the number materially. In rough order of leverage: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Cap the budget — a hard ceiling, not a hope⌄ Set a per-run or per-user token/dollar cap that HARD-STOPS the agent. Because the same task can cost 30x more on a bad run, a ceiling is the only thing that bounds the tail. Most agent harnesses expose a max-tokens or max-steps limit — use it. This is the single most important control. ←PreviousNext→ 2Cache the stable prefix⌄ The system prompt, tool definitions, and house rules are re-sent on every loop step (the snowball). Prompt caching charges those repeated tokens at a fraction of the input rate. On a long agentic run this is often the biggest single saving, because the cached part is exactly what gets re-read the most. ←PreviousNext→ 3Route by model tier⌄ Don't run one frontier model for the whole loop. Use a cheap, fast model (Haiku-class, or a small open model) for the grunt work — reading files, formatting, routine tool calls — and reserve the expensive frontier model for the hard reasoning or the orchestrator role. Orchestrator-worker splits with cheaper workers cut cost 40–60% in production benchmarks at near-parity accuracy. ←PreviousNext→ 4Prune the context aggressively⌄ The snowball is the problem, so shrink it. Compact old turns, drop tool outputs the agent no longer needs, summarize instead of carrying raw transcripts, and start fresh sub-tasks with a clean context instead of one ever-growing thread. Every token you remove is a token you stop paying for on EVERY remaining step. ←PreviousNext→ Audit a runaway agent (paste your run's token breakdown) CopyOpen in Claude↗ You are a cost engineer. Here is a token-usage breakdown of one agentic run (input vs output tokens per step, tool calls, model used). Diagnose where the money went, in priority order: 1. Is input or output driving cost? (Agents are almost always input-heavy.) 2. Which repeated content should be prompt-CACHED (system prompt, tools, rules)? 3. Which steps could run on a CHEAPER model without losing correctness? 4. Where is context snowballing — what can be pruned, compacted, or summarized? 5. What is a safe per-run token CAP that stops the worst tail without hurting the median run? Give me the estimated % saving per fix and the ONE change to make first.
documents.s: The four levers that actually cut the bill

documents.t: The cheapest agentic run is the one you don't make. If a task is a single, well-specified transformation — summarize this, classify that, rewrite this — a plain chat/completion call does it at a fraction of the cost, with no snowball at all. Reach for an agent when the work genuinely requires reading, deciding, acting, and re-checking in a loop against a changing environment (explore a repo, debug across files, drive a browser). If you can write the exact steps yourself, script them — don't pay a model to re-derive them every run. flipTermContext snowballDefinitionThe accumulated transcript an agent re-reads on every loop step. Beginner One of AI's most meaningful uses gets the least attention: as an assistive tool. Claude can adapt information to you — your pace, your format, your language — which can be genuinely leveling.
documents.s: Accessibility: Claude as an Assistive Tool

documents.t: Dyslexia / reading load — "rewrite this in short, simple sentences," "summarize the key points," "explain this in plain language." Low vision — pair with voice mode to listen and dictate; ask for clean, well-structured text that screen readers handle well. If you use the CLI, Claude Code has a dedicated screen reader mode and accessibility settings. Neurodivergence / focus (ADHD, etc.) — "break this into a checklist," "what's the one next step?", turn a wall of text into a clear plan, draft the email you're stuck on. Language learners — translate, simplify, explain idioms, practice conversation, or get the same idea at different difficulty levels. Anxiety around writing — get a non-judgmental first draft to react to, lowering the barrier to starting.

Rewrite this so it's easy to read: short sentences, simple words, one idea per line. Keep all the meaning. Text: {paste} Turn this into a step-by-step checklist with the single most important step marked. {paste} Explain this in {your language}, then give me 3 phrases to practice.

It's an aid, not a clinician. For health/medical/legal decisions, consult a professional — verify anything important (Responsible Use). Voice and mobile make it available wherever you are (Voice Mode, Mobile). Your data is yours — share only what you're comfortable with (Privacy). :::tip The site itself AILmanac aims to be accessible too — clear language, level badges, keyboard-navigable, good contrast. Found an accessibility issue? Tell us. :::

All levels For founders and small teams, AI is leverage: it does the work of a junior marketer, analyst, and assistant at once. Direct it well and keep judgment on the things that matter.

Positioning & messaging — nail the value prop, then derive copy from it. Marketing content — landing pages, emails, ads, social, FAQs (see Writing). Customer comms — draft replies, handle complaints, write announcements. Research — market/competitor scans (verify!), customer-interview question sets. Planning — turn goals into prioritized, time-boxed plans. Docs & ops — SOPs, job posts, meeting summaries.

Before any copy, get the one-liner right: Write 3 versions of a value proposition using: for {audience} who {need}, {product} is a {category} that {key benefit}, unlike {alternative}. Then critique each in one line. Everything downstream (ads, emails, landing pages) gets easier once this is sharp.

:::warning Don't fabricate proof, and mind the claims Never invent testimonials, metrics, case studies, or awards — use [insert real number] placeholders and fill them with real data. Watch regulated or unsubstantiated claims (health, finance, "#1", guarantees). Verify market facts and figures before acting (Hallucinations). Protect data — don't paste customer PII or confidential numbers into unvetted tools (Privacy). :::

Advanced Last verified: 2026-09-23. Runner concurrency caps, queue timeouts and merge-queue settings are platform limits that GitHub changes without much noise. The mechanisms below are stable; re-check the exact numbers against the limits page before you size a pipeline on them. Confirm against the official source. What you'll learn Know why the merge queue — not the runner budget — is the first thing that breaks under agent PR volume Do the batching arithmetic: how a few points of failure rate collapse speculative merging Rank the four levers correctly, because 'add more runners' is the weakest one Ship a gate that proves an agent's test actually fails without the agent's fix Quarantine flakes on evidence instead of vibes, and know the caching gotcha that silently poisons CI Your coding agents work. That is the problem. A team that merged 5 pull requests a day and now merges 40 has not changed its test suite, its runner budget, or its branch protection rules. It has changed the arrival rate into a queueing system that was tuned for the old one. Everything downstream — merge queue, flaky-test noise, runner concurrency, review attention — was sized for human throughput, and queueing systems do not degrade gracefully. They hold, hold, hold, then fall over inside a week. This page is the pipeline side of the verification bottleneck. That page asks who checks the code. This one asks whether your CI can physically absorb the volume, and what to do when it can't.

−7.2%. DORA's 2024 Accelerate State of DevOps report modelled a 25% increase in AI adoption and estimated a 7.2% decrease in delivery stability alongside a 1.5% decrease in throughput. Individual productivity and job satisfaction went up. Delivery-level outcomes went down — the report ties this to larger changesets and weaker batching discipline. The 2025 follow-up reframes it: AI is an amplifier, magnifying whatever your delivery system already is. A pipeline that was fragile at 5 PRs/day becomes unusable at 40. 19%. METR's randomised trial (July 2025) took 16 experienced open-source maintainers and 246 real issues from their own repositories, randomising whether AI tools were allowed. With AI, tasks took 19% longer. The gap that matters for CI planning is the perceptual one: developers predicted a 24% speed-up, and after the slowdown still believed they had been sped up by 20%. Nobody on your team will tell you the pipeline is the constraint, because nobody experiences it as one — they experience it as "waiting", which feels like weather. 1.5% / 16% / 84%. Google's published flakiness data: roughly 1.5% of test runs report a flaky result; about 16% of their 4.2M tests have shown flakiness at some point; and around 84% of observed pass→fail transitions involve a flaky test rather than a real regression. Hold onto that 1.5% — it is small enough to ignore at 5 PRs/day and load-bearing at 40.
documents.s: Three numbers that frame the whole problem

documents.t: Most teams assume the ceiling is compute. It isn't. It's the merge queue, and the reason is a mechanism most people have never read the docs for. GitHub's merge queue does speculative checking. Queue PRs #1, #2, #3 and it builds temporary branches: main + #1, main + #1 + #2, main + #1 + #2 + #3 — and tests all of them in parallel. If every check passes, all three land in one round. That is the whole value proposition: batching turns N serial validations into one. Now read the failure path. When a check fails for the group containing PR #1, GitHub removes #1 from the queue — and every group behind it contained #1's changes, so those groups are invalid and get rebuilt without it. One bad PR does not cost you one slot. It costs you the rest of the batch's CI round. That makes queue throughput a function of your pass rate, and it's steeper than intuition suggests. Model it: batch size N, each PR independently failing with probability p, and you merge the run of PRs up to the first failure. Expected merges per round is a geometric expectation: E[merges] = (1 − p) · (1 − (1 − p)^N) / p With N = 10: Per-PR failure rate p Expected merges per round Rounds to clear 10 PRs 2% 8.9 ~1.1 5% 7.6 ~1.3 10% 5.9 ~1.7 20% 3.6 ~2.8 30% 2.3 ~4.4 Two consequences most teams get backwards: A flaky suite is a throughput tax, not a nuisance tax. Flakiness adds directly to p. Going from 5% real failures to 5% real + 5% flake takes you from 7.6 merges per round to 5.9 — roughly 23% of your merge capacity, lost to tests that were never testing anything. Raising the batch size is the wrong lever when p is high. Bigger N only helps when (1 − p)^N stays near 1. At p = 0.2, a batch of 10 delivers 3.6 merges; the fix is lowering p, not queueing more optimism. And agent volume pushes p the wrong way — DORA's stability finding is exactly a statement about p rising.
documents.s: Why the merge queue breaks first

documents.t: Do this on a napkin before you buy runners. Assumptions stated, because they're what make it wrong for your team: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Count job-minutes, not wall-clock⌄ A 45-minute suite fanned out into 15 parallel jobs still costs ~45 job-minutes. Parallelism buys latency, never cost. Take your suite's total job-minutes from a recent run, not from the slowest job. ←PreviousNext→ 2Multiply by validations per PR, not by PRs⌄ With a merge queue every PR is validated at least twice: once on the PR branch, once inside a merge group. Reruns and rebuilds from the p-math above add more. Budget 2.5x as a floor, not 1x. ←PreviousNext→ 3Divide by the burst window, not the day⌄ 40 PRs x 2.5 validations x 45 job-min = 4,500 job-minutes. Spread over 24 hours that is trivial. It does not arrive over 24 hours — it arrives in two or three hours around review time. 4,500 job-min into a 2-hour window needs ~37 sustained concurrent jobs. ←PreviousNext→ 4Compare against your plan's hard ceiling⌄ GitHub-hosted standard runners cap total concurrent jobs at 20 (Free), 40 (Pro), 60 (Team) and 500 (Enterprise). The napkin above quietly exceeds Free and sits on top of Pro — during the burst, which is the only window that matters. ←PreviousNext→ 5Find the silent failure⌄ A queued job is cancelled after 24 hours. On a saturated queue this shows up as jobs that never ran rather than jobs that failed, which is far harder to notice and does not page anyone. ←PreviousNext→ The takeaway is not "buy Enterprise". It's that the constraint is burst concurrency, and the daily-average number that makes your pipeline look fine is the number hiding the problem.

Teams reach for these in almost exactly the reverse of the useful order. 1. Lower p (highest leverage, lowest cost). Every point of failure rate removed pays off nonlinearly in the batching math. Concretely: make agents run the fast suite locally before opening a PR, require a green pre-merge check before a PR is allowed into the queue, and quarantine flakes aggressively (below). This costs no compute. 2. Cut the work per validation — test selection. This is the only lever that changes the exponent rather than the constant. Instead of running everything, run what the change can plausibly break: Develocity Predictive Test Selection builds a model from your own Build Scan history plus cross-project patterns, and ships a simulator so you can measure the savings and the missed-failure rate before enabling it. Two safety details worth stealing even if you never buy it: you can pin must-run tests by class pattern or annotation, and it always selects recently flaky tests, because a flaky test is by definition unpredictable from the change. Pair it with a "remaining tests" run post-merge or nightly so nothing is skipped forever. Bazel / Buck2 get this structurally: the build graph knows which targets depend on the changed files, so bazel test on affected targets is target determination for free. No build graph? Python has pytest-testmon, which records which tests cover which code and re-runs only the affected ones. Jest ships --changedSince out of the box. Test selection, three ecosystems CopyOpen in Claude↗ # Bazel — test only what the diff can reach bazel test $(bazel query "rdeps(//..., set($(git diff --name-only origin/main)))" --output=label 2>/dev/null) # Python — coverage-based impact analysis pip install pytest-testmon pytest --testmon # first run builds the DB, later runs select # Jest — built in, no plugin npx jest --changedSince=origin/main 3. Cache aggressively — and know the gotcha. Remote caching stores action results keyed by a hash of inputs, command line and whitelisted environment. Bazel's own docs flag the trap: tools outside the workspace are not tracked, so two machines with different compiler versions can get a cache hit on work that would have produced different outputs. Whitelist what matters with --action_env, and keep write access to CI only — developer machines should read: Remote cache, CI-writes-only CopyOpen in Claude↗ # CI: read and write bazel test //... --remote_cache=grpcs://cache.internal:443 # Developer machines: read only, never poison the shared cache bazel test //... --remote_cache=grpcs://cache.internal:443 \ --remote_upload_local_results=false 4. Add runners (last). Linear cost, linear benefit, and it does nothing about p. Do it after the first three, when you actually know your burst concurrency number.

Everything above applies to any high-volume pipeline. This one is specific to agent-written code, and it is the gap most CI setups have. When the same agent writes the fix and the test for the fix, "tests pass" carries much less information than you think. Two failure shapes show up constantly: The test asserts the behaviour of the implementation rather than the requirement — it passes because it was written by reading the code it is testing. The agent, when a pre-existing test fails, edits the test to match the new behaviour instead of fixing the code. The diff is green and the regression shipped. That behaviour has a name and a literature — see reward hacking in coding agents for why models do it and which defenses have measured effect sizes. What follows is the pipeline-side control, not the model-side one. The cheap structural gate: a new test must fail against the pre-change code. That's the red-green discipline of TDD turned into a machine check, and it's what mutation testing formalises at scale. You do not need a mutation-testing framework to get most of the value — you need one CI job: CI gate: new tests must fail without the change CopyOpen in Claude↗ #!/usr/bin/env bash # must-fail-first.sh — run in CI on PRs that add tests set -euo pipefail NEW_TESTS=$(git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD -- 'tests/**' 'test/**') [ -z "$NEW_TESTS" ] && { echo "no new tests, skipping"; exit 0; } # Keep the new tests, revert everything else to the base commit git stash push --keep-index -- $NEW_TESTS git checkout origin/main -- src/ git stash pop # The new tests MUST fail now. If they pass, they prove nothing. if pytest $NEW_TESTS -q; then echo "FAIL: new tests pass against unmodified source — they do not test the change." exit 1 fi echo "OK: new tests fail without the fix." Two honest caveats. It only works when source and tests live in separate trees, and a test that fails for the wrong reason (import error, missing fixture) passes this gate. It is a floor, not a proof — but it catches the single most common way an agent-authored PR is green and worthless. The complementary review-side control is a reviewer that doesn't share the author's context: see the hybrid AI code reviewer and the PR-review GitHub Action.
documents.s: The AI-specific failure mode: the agent grades its own homework

documents.t: Given 84% of pass→fail transitions are flakes, "rerun it" is the default human response and it is the most expensive one available — it burns a full validation on a test that was never going to tell you anything. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Measure before you judge⌄ A flaky test is one that produces different results on the same commit. Run the suite N times on an unchanged main and record per-test failure counts. That is your evidence; developer memory is not. ←PreviousNext→ 2Quarantine on a threshold, not an argument⌄ Anything above your threshold moves to a non-blocking job that still runs and still reports. It stops gating merges immediately — that is the throughput win — and it stays visible so it does not become dead code. ←PreviousNext→ 3Cap the quarantine and give it an owner⌄ An uncapped quarantine is a graveyard. Fixed budget (say 1% of tests), a name attached, an expiry date. Over budget means the next flake evicts the oldest one back into blocking. ←PreviousNext→ 4Never let test selection skip a flake⌄ This is the counter-intuitive rule Develocity encodes: recently-flaky tests are always selected, because the model cannot predict them from the diff. Selecting away your flakes hides the signal you need to fix them. ←PreviousNext→ 5Re-derive p after each round⌄ Recompute your per-PR failure rate monthly and put it on the dashboard next to merge-queue throughput. It is the one number that tells you whether the pipeline is getting better or the agents are just getting louder. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: Flake quarantine that survives contact with agents

documents.t: merge_group is not automatic. GitHub's docs are explicit: you must add the merge_group event to your workflow triggers, or your checks never fire inside the queue and merges fail on missing required checks. This is the single most common merge-queue misconfiguration. The 24-hour queue cancellation is silent. Saturated queue → jobs vanish rather than fail. Alert on queue depth, not just on red builds. Matrix jobs cap at 256 per workflow run. Generated matrices (a common agent-scaffolding pattern) hit this without a useful error. Cross-machine cache hits can be wrong. Untracked external toolchains produce false hits. Pin toolchains, whitelist environment with --action_env. Branch protection with wildcard patterns is incompatible with merge queues. If your protection rules use wildcards, the queue will not engage. Agent PRs touching CI are a security boundary, not a style question. A PR that can edit workflow files can exfiltrate CI secrets — see GitHub issue → CI secrets and hardening autonomous runs.
documents.s: Gotchas that cost a day each

documents.t: There is no configuration that makes a pipeline absorb unbounded agent output. What the levers above buy you is a system whose cost grows with the size of the change rather than the number of pull requests — test selection and caching are sublinear, runners are linear, and merge-queue batching is only sublinear while your pass rate stays high. Which puts the real constraint back where DORA's 2025 framing puts it: AI amplifies the delivery system you already have. If small batches, fast suites and low flakiness were already your practice, agents make you much faster. If they weren't, agents find out. Check yourself 0/6 1Your merge queue has batch size 10 and your per-PR failure rate rises from 5% to 20%. Roughly what happens to expected merges per round? It drops slightly, from about 9 to about 8It roughly halves, from about 7.6 to about 3.6It is unchanged — batching absorbs failuresIt doubles, because failures free up queue slots 2A merge group fails because of PR #1. What does GitHub do to the groups queued behind it? Nothing — they were tested independently and merge as-isIt merges them anyway and opens a revert PR for #1It removes #1 and rebuilds the groups behind it without #1's changesIt clears the entire queue and every author must re-queue 3Which lever changes how CI cost scales, rather than just shifting the constant? Adding more concurrent runnersIncreasing the merge-queue batch sizeTest selection driven by what the diff can reachRetrying failed jobs automatically 4Why does Develocity's Predictive Test Selection always run recently flaky tests, even when the diff does not touch them? Flaky tests are usually the slowest, so they parallelise wellA flaky test's outcome is not predictable from the change, so the model cannot safely skip itContractual compliance requirements demand full suitesFlaky tests have the highest historical code coverage 5An agent's PR adds a fix and a test, and CI is green. What does the 'must fail first' gate check? That the new test achieves at least 80% line coverageThat the new test fails when run against the pre-change sourceThat the agent did not modify any existing test filesThat the test runs in under one second 6Two machines get a Bazel remote cache hit on the same action but would produce different outputs. What is the most likely cause? The content-addressable store dropped an output fileOne machine used --disk_cache and the other did notA toolchain outside the workspace differs and is not part of the action hashThe action cache stores only stdout, never metadata flipTermSpeculative checking (merge queue)DefinitionGitHub builds temporary branches for base+PR1, base+PR1+PR2, … and tests them in parallel. All green means the whole batch lands in one round. A failure removes that PR and forces every group behind it to be rebuilt.Press Enter or Space to flip the card. Use the left and right arrow keys to move between cards.Term shown. ←Prev 1 / 12 Next→ Key takeaways The merge queue breaks before the runner budget does. Speculative batching is a bet on your pass rate, and one failing PR invalidates every group behind it. Compute E[merges] = (1 − p)(1 − (1 − p)^N)/p once for your real numbers. It turns 'CI feels slow' into a decision about which lever to pull. Flakiness is throughput, not hygiene. At Google's published rates the noise is bigger than the signal — 84% of pass→fail transitions are flakes. Size for burst concurrency, never daily average. The daily number is the one hiding the problem, and a saturated queue cancels jobs silently at 24 hours. Test selection is the only sublinear lever: Bazel/Buck2 target determination, Develocity PTS with its simulator, pytest-testmon, or jest --changedSince. When the agent writes both the fix and the test, green means less than you think. Gate on the test failing against pre-change source. DORA's framing holds: AI amplifies the delivery system you already have. Small batches, fast suites and low flake were always the advice — agents just made ignoring it expensive.

The Verification Bottleneck — why review, not typing, became the constraint GitHub Action that reviews every PR — the concrete workflow to put in front of this pipeline Evaluating your AI agent — the eval gate that belongs in the same CI run

All levels What you'll learn Know what AI coding is genuinely great at — explain, generate, refactor, debug, translate, review Run the golden loop: context in, plan, generate, read, run — and loop failures back as fresh context Reach for prompts that pull their weight instead of vague one-liners Internalize the two hard rules: verify by running, and never paste secrets Whether you're learning to code or shipping production software, AI changes the loop. The winners treat it as a fast, knowledgeable pair — and verify everything it produces.

Explain unfamiliar code or errors in plain language. Generate boilerplate, tests, and first drafts of functions. Refactor for clarity, and debug by reasoning about a stack trace. Translate between languages/frameworks. Review a diff for bugs and smells. For real codebases, do this in your repo with Claude Code, which can read files, run tests, and edit with your approval.

Give context — the relevant code, the error, what you expected vs. got. Vague in, vague out. Ask for a plan on non-trivial changes before edits (Plan Mode). Generate the change. Read it — understand before you accept. You own the code. Run it — tests/lint/build. Never trust "this works" without running it. The step that separates good results from bad ones is the arrow back to the top: when a test fails, you don't patch blindly — you feed the failure back in as fresh context.

Explain code + spot the edge cases CopyOpen in Claude↗ Explain what this function does and any edge cases it mishandles: {code} Generate tests CopyOpen in Claude↗ Write tests for {function}. Cover the happy path and the edge cases. {code} Debug from a stack trace CopyOpen in Claude↗ This throws {error}. Here's the code and stack trace. Find the root cause and propose a minimal fix. {context}

:::warning Verify, and protect your secrets Run and review generated code — it can be subtly wrong or invent APIs that don't exist. Never paste secrets/keys into a prompt (Privacy). For agentic/automated coding, lock down permissions and read Securing Agents. ::: Check yourself 0/3 1In the golden loop, what most separates good AI-coding results from bad ones? Always using the largest model availableThe arrow back to the top: feeding a failed test's output back in as fresh context instead of patching blindlyAccepting the first generation to save time 2Why read generated code before you accept it? Reading is what triggers the test runnerIt can be subtly wrong or invent APIs that don't exist — and you own the code either wayThe SDK refuses to run code you haven't opened 3Which of these should never go into a prompt? The error message and stack traceSecrets or API keysWhat you expected versus what actually happened Key takeaways Treat AI as a fast, knowledgeable pair — then verify everything it produces by actually running it Context in, quality out: give the code, the error, and expected-vs-actual, never a vague ask Ask for a plan before non-trivial edits so you review the approach before any code changes Read generated code before accepting — it can be subtly wrong or invent APIs that don't exist Never paste secrets or keys into a prompt, and lock down permissions before letting an agent code on its own
What Claude Code Is Customize Claude Code for a Real Repo Your First API Call
All levels You don't need to be a data scientist to get answers from data with AI — but you do need to keep it honest. AI writes the query and explains the result; you confirm the numbers are real.

Write SQL / spreadsheet formulas / pandas from a plain-language question. Explain what a query or result means in business terms. Clean & transform messy data (describe the mess, get steps). Suggest the right chart for the question. Interpret output and propose the next question.

Describe your data — columns, types, and the grain (one row = ?). Don't assume names. State the question the analysis should answer. Get the query + a one-line explanation of what it does and its assumptions. Run it yourself on the real data. Bring results back for plain-language interpretation and caveats. My table `orders` has columns: order_id, customer_id, created_at, total_eur, status. One row per order. Write SQL for monthly revenue from completed orders in 2025, and explain any assumptions.

:::warning Never trust numbers it didn't compute If the AI states a result without running the query on your data, that number may be invented. Run queries yourself; treat any figure you didn't compute as unverified. And remember correlation ≠ causation — ask it to flag associational claims. See Hallucinations. ::: Sanity-check magnitudes — implausible result? investigate, don't publish. State assumptions (nulls, dedup, time zones, currency). Don't paste sensitive/PII data into tools you haven't vetted (Privacy).

Advanced Last verified: 2026-07-24. Anthropic's evaluation guide is the source of truth for methodology (SMART criteria, exact-match, LLM-graded Likert/binary). Agent-trajectory eval is an emerging discipline — treat framework names as illustrative and confirm APIs at each vendor's docs. Confirm against the official source. What you'll learn Understand why agent evals differ from prompt evals — trajectory matters, not just the final answer Build a golden set of 20–100 real cases with clear pass criteria Score four layers: tool-call correctness, trajectory quality, task success, production drift Use LLM-as-judge safely: rubric first, calibrate against humans, spot-check verdicts Ship an eval that runs in CI and fails a bad change before it reaches users An agent eval answers a harder question than "did the prompt return the right words?" It asks: did a model running in a loop pick the right tools, in the right order, with the right arguments, arrive at the right outcome — and stay within budget and safety bounds? Skip this step and you'll ship a "helpful" agent that quietly regresses every time you tweak the system prompt.

A single-prompt eval scores one input → one output. An agent produces a trajectory: a chain of reasoning, tool calls, intermediate observations, and revisions across many turns. Two failure modes make this hard: Right answer, wrong path. The agent stumbles onto the correct output after wasteful loops, unsafe actions, or lucky guesses. Final-answer-only evals mark this a pass; production won't. Wrong answer, plausible path. Every step looks reasonable in isolation, but the agent misused a tool, ignored a constraint, or hallucinated an intermediate fact. You need to look at the trace, not just the reply.
documents.s: Why agents need their own evals

documents.t: Layer them cheapest-first so a bad change fails fast without waiting for expensive graders. Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Layer 1 — Tool-call correctness (deterministic)⌄ For each expected step, check tool name matches, required parameters are present, and types validate. Pure code, milliseconds, no model needed. Catches 'called search when it should have called write_file' before anything else runs. ←PreviousNext→ 2Layer 2 — Trajectory quality (rubric + LLM-judge)⌄ Score the full trace: did the agent take a sensible path, or wander, loop, or backtrack? Number of steps vs. minimum needed, redundant calls, retries after tool errors, whether it stopped when done. Use an LLM judge with an explicit rubric here. ←PreviousNext→ 3Layer 3 — Task success (end-to-end)⌄ Did the goal get met? Deterministic where possible (schema valid, file written, test passes), LLM-judged where fuzzy (summary faithful, answer helpful). This is your headline number. ←PreviousNext→ 4Layer 4 — Production drift & safety⌄ In prod, sample real traces and re-grade a slice. Watch intervention rate (how often a human had to step in), refusal rate, and cost per successful task. When these shift, your model, tools, or inputs changed underneath you. ←PreviousNext→

Not every metric belongs on the dashboard. These five drive shipping decisions in 2026: Metric What it measures Why it matters Task success rate % of golden-set cases the agent finishes correctly The headline. Everything else is diagnostic. Cost per successful task $ / passing case (tokens in + out, tool costs) Success at 10× the cost is a regression. Latency (p50 / p95) Wall-clock per task, tail included p95 is what real users feel — averages lie. Tool-call accuracy % of expected tool calls with correct name + args Predicts trajectory quality; cheap to compute. Intervention rate % of tasks needing human takeover in prod The autonomy number. Rising = trust falling. Track them together — one moving without the others is usually a leading signal, not noise.

Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Mine real inputs⌄ Pull 20–100 tasks from actual usage (logs, support tickets, user requests). Cover the frequent easy path, the tricky middle, and the edge cases that already bit you. ←PreviousNext→ 2Write pass criteria per case⌄ For each: what does 'done' look like? Exact expected output, required facts, valid JSON schema, files that must exist, or a rubric for fuzzy cases. If you can't write the criterion, the case is unusable — cut or clarify it. ←PreviousNext→ 3Annotate the ideal trajectory⌄ For a subset, sketch the tool sequence a good agent would take. This is what Layer 1 checks against. ←PreviousNext→ 4Freeze it, version it⌄ Commit the set to your repo. Never edit a case in place — add v2 alongside v1 so score history stays comparable. ←PreviousNext→ 5Grow it from failures⌄ Every prod bug becomes a new eval case before you fix it. That's how the set stays predictive instead of decaying. ←PreviousNext→

Grading fuzzy outputs by hand doesn't scale. A capable model reading against an explicit rubric does — Anthropic's own eval methodology guide recommends this pattern for tone, faithfulness, helpfulness, and safety. Judges have well-documented biases: they prefer longer answers, the first option shown, and outputs that echo their own phrasing. Three habits keep them honest: Rubric, not vibes. "Rate helpfulness 1–5" is useless. Anchor every point on the scale to observable behavior. Calibrate on a human-labeled sample. Have humans grade 30–50 cases; measure judge-vs-human agreement (aim for Cohen's κ ≥ 0.6). If it disagrees, tighten the rubric. Use a different model as judge. Grading with the same model that produced the output leaks bias in both directions. Spot-check verdicts weekly. Read 10 random judge scores and their reasoning. It's the cheapest way to catch drift. LLM-as-judge rubric template CopyOpen in Claude↗ You are grading an AI assistant's response against a rubric. Be strict. Cite exact evidence from the response. <task>{task}</task> <response>{response}</response> Rubric (rate 1–5 per dimension): - Task completion: 1 = ignored task; 3 = partial; 5 = fully done, no gaps. - Faithfulness: 1 = contains false claims; 3 = mostly grounded, one soft claim; 5 = every claim traceable to input/tools. - Efficiency: 1 = wandered/looped; 3 = extra steps; 5 = minimum viable path. Output JSON only: {"task_completion": N, "faithfulness": N, "efficiency": N, "evidence": "<quote>", "verdict": "pass"|"fail"} Trajectory review prompt (Layer 2) CopyOpen in Claude↗ You are auditing an AI agent's tool-call trajectory. The goal was: {goal} Expected minimum steps: {n_min} <trajectory> {list of tool_name(args) -> result, in order} </trajectory> Answer in JSON: {"steps_taken": N, "wasted_steps": N, "wrong_tool_calls": [<indices>], "unsafe_actions": [<indices>], "verdict": "pass"|"fail", "reason": "<one sentence>"} Adversarial case generator (grow the set) CopyOpen in Claude↗ Generate 5 new eval cases that are likely to break an agent whose current failures cluster around: {failure_pattern}. For each case give: input, expected output OR pass criterion, ideal tool sequence, and why this case is hard. Return YAML.
documents.s: LLM-as-judge — cheap, fast, but calibrate it

documents.t: The eval only pays off when it blocks regressions automatically. Wire it into CI as a check on every prompt / model / tool change: # tests/eval_gate.py — runs on every PR import json, sys from anthropic import Anthropic from my_agent import run_agent client = Anthropic() golden = json.load(open("evals/golden.v3.json")) results = [] for case in golden: trace = run_agent(case["input"]) layer1 = tool_calls_match(trace, case["expected_tools"]) # deterministic layer3 = judge(client, case, trace.final_output) # LLM rubric results.append({"id": case["id"], "layer1": layer1, "layer3": layer3["verdict"]}) pass_rate = sum(r["layer3"] == "pass" for r in results) / len(results) tool_acc = sum(r["layer1"] for r in results) / len(results) # Gates — tighten over time assert pass_rate >= 0.85, f"Task success dropped to {pass_rate:.0%}" assert tool_acc >= 0.90, f"Tool-call accuracy dropped to {tool_acc:.0%}" print(f"PASS: task={pass_rate:.0%} tools={tool_acc:.0%}") Store per-run scores so you can chart the trend. A drop of 3+ points between merges is a real regression, not noise. Anti-patterns that make evals under-deliver Judging the final answer only — misses every trajectory bug. Score Layers 1 and 2 too. Static golden set — if it doesn't grow with every prod failure it stops predicting prod. Budget time monthly. Same model as agent and judge — bias in both directions. Rotate to a different model for grading. No cost or latency in the gate — a prompt tweak that adds 8 tool calls can 'pass' the eval while 10×-ing the bill. Vibes-only scoring — 'feels better' is not a metric. If you can't diff two numbers, you can't ship confidently. Key takeaways Agents produce trajectories, not answers — evaluate the path, not only the outcome Layer cheapest-first: tool-call correctness → trajectory quality → task success → production drift The five metrics that ship decisions: task success rate, cost per success, p50/p95 latency, tool-call accuracy, intervention rate LLM-as-judge scales, but only with an explicit rubric, a different model, and calibration against human labels A golden set that doesn't grow from prod failures stops predicting prod — grow it monthly Wire the eval into CI as a hard gate — the check that catches a regression before users do
documents.s: CI gate: fail the bad change before it ships

documents.t: Check yourself 0/4 1Why do agents need trajectory evals, not just final-answer evals? Final-answer evals are too slow to run in CIAn agent can arrive at the right answer via wandering or unsafe steps (right answer, wrong path) — and produce a plausible-looking path to a wrong answerTrajectory evals are the only kind that support LLM-as-judgeFinal-answer evals only work for classification tasks 2You're layering your evals. Which order is cheapest-to-most-expensive and correct? LLM-judged task success → deterministic tool-call checks → production drift → trajectory rubricDeterministic tool-call correctness → trajectory quality (LLM-judge) → task success → production driftProduction drift → task success → trajectory rubric → tool-call checksTrajectory rubric → task success → tool-call checks → production drift 3Which pair of habits actually keeps LLM-as-judge trustworthy over time? Grade with the same model as the agent, and rewrite the rubric each runUse a rubric with observable anchors, and calibrate the judge against a human-labeled samplePrefer vibes-based prompts to avoid over-specifying, and never spot-check verdictsAlways use the largest available model as judge, no calibration needed 4Your CI gate passes task success rate but latency and cost per task doubled. What's the right call? Ship it — task success is the headline metricFail the gate: the five shipping metrics move together, and a 2× cost/latency change is a regression even if pass rate heldRerun the eval — the numbers must be noiseLoosen the pass-rate threshold to justify shipping flipTermTrajectory (in agent evals)DefinitionThe full ordered chain of tool calls, arguments, observations, and reasoning steps an agent takes across a task — the thing you evaluate in addition to the final output.Press Enter or Space to flip the card. All levels AI can be the patient, infinitely-available tutor most of us never had — if you use it to understand, not to outsource thinking. The difference between learning and cheating is the workflow.

Explain like I'm new. "Explain [concept] simply, with one analogy and one example." Then go deeper in layers. Socratic tutoring. "Don't give me the answer — ask me questions that lead me to it." Teach-back. Explain it, then you restate it; the AI corrects your gaps. This is where real learning sticks. Quiz me. "Generate 5 questions on [topic], then grade my answers and explain the misses." Study plan. "I have 2 weeks for [exam]. Build a plan and drill my weak spots."

Tutor me on {topic}. Start by asking what I already know, then teach one step at a time and check my understanding before moving on. Don't just give answers. I'll explain {concept} back to you. Point out anything wrong or missing, kindly and specifically. Here's my explanation: {your attempt}

:::warning For graded work, get guidance — not the answer key If you paste homework and copy the output, you didn't learn it (and may break your school's rules). Ask for hints, checks, and explanations that get you to the answer. Own the result. ::: Verify facts — tutors can be confidently wrong; cross-check key claims (Hallucinations). One concept at a time — depth beats breadth. Spaced practice — come back and re-quiz; that's what makes it stick.
documents.s: Use it to learn, not to cheat

Beginner Five things almost anyone can use today. Each comes with a starter prompt — paste it, swap the brackets, refine in plain language.

"Here's an email I received. Draft a polite, concise reply that [accepts the meeting but proposes Thursday instead]. Keep it under 80 words. Email: [paste]" Follow-ups that help: "more formal," "add a line thanking them," "give me two versions."

"Summarise this in 5 bullet points a busy manager could read in 30 seconds, then list any decisions or action items separately. Text: [paste]" Works on articles, meeting notes, threads, and reports. For very long inputs, ask for the summary first, then drill in.

"I need to [organise a 30-person team offsite] by [October]. Give me a step-by-step plan with rough timing, and flag the 3 things most likely to go wrong." Great for project plans, checklists, and turning a vague goal into next actions.

"I'm deciding between [option A] and [option B] for [situation]. Lay out the trade-offs in a table, then tell me what else I should consider before deciding." Use it as a sparring partner — ask it to argue the opposite case to pressure-test your thinking.

"Write a first draft of [a LinkedIn post announcing our new feature]. Match this voice: [paste a paragraph you wrote]. Then suggest a punchier opening line." Giving a sample of your writing is the secret to outputs that don't sound generic.

:::tip Give context, then iterate Every prompt above names the goal, format, and constraints — that's Prompting Basics. And none of them have to be right first try; refine in plain language. ::: :::warning Verify anything factual Dates, numbers, names, quotes, and "facts" can be confidently wrong. For anything that matters, check it — see Hallucinations. :::

All levels AI is a superb research accelerator — and a dangerous one if you trust it blindly. Used right, it compresses hours of reading into minutes; used carelessly, it confidently invents sources. Here's the disciplined version.

Summarize a long document/paper into key points + implications. Compare multiple sources into a table (what they agree/disagree on). Build a landscape — map the players, approaches, or arguments on a topic. Extract specific facts/figures from a document (with citations). Pressure-test — "what's the strongest counterargument to this?"

Using ONLY the text I provide, summarize the key findings and quote the exact sentence supporting each one. If something isn't in the text, say "not stated." Text: """{paste}""" Feed it the sources. Don't ask it to recall facts from memory for anything important — paste the material or use a tool that retrieves it (RAG). Demand citations. "Quote the sentence that supports each claim." Unsupported claims become visible. Separate fact from inference. Ask it to label what's stated vs. interpreted. :::warning Fabricated citations are the classic trap Models invent realistic-looking papers, authors, and URLs. Verify every citation exists before you rely on it. See Hallucinations. :::

Gather sources yourself (or via a retrieval tool). Summarize each with grounding + citations. Synthesize across them into a themed comparison. Identify gaps/disagreements and the "so what." Spot-check the critical facts against the originals.
